Another formulation is a parabolic distribution for \(A_z\) (Engelund, 1978):

\[ u_t = \kappa u_* z\left(1- rac{z}{H} ight) ag{2-81} \]

For compatibility with the original model formulation, the computed value of \(A_z\) is corrected using the Mamayev formulation:

\[ u_t = \max\left( u, u_{t_{PARAB}}e^{-CRi} ight) ag{2-82} \]

docs.title: W2N Formulation
docs.text:
The W2N formulation is the same as the W2 model except that the mixing length is no longer the layer thickness but is computed using Nickuradse's mixing length model. The equations for the W2N formulation are:

\[ A_z = \kappa\left(\frac{\ell_m^2}{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\tau_{wy}e^{-2kz}}{\rho A_z}\right)^2}\;e^{-CRi} \tag{2-83} \] \[ \ell_m = H\left[0.14 - 0.08\left(1-\frac{z}{H}\right)^2 - 0.06\left(1-\frac{z}{H}\right)^4\right] \tag{2-84} \]

docs.title: TKE Formulation
docs.text:
The Turbulent Kinetic Energy (TKE) formulation is an application of the k-ε turbulence model. This model includes vertical transport of kinetic energy and dissipation by advection and diffusion, as well as horizontal transport by advection. The model solves two partial differential equations for \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) to compute the turbulent eddy viscosity:

\[ u_t = C_\mu rac{k^2}{\varepsilon} ag{2-85} \] \[ rac{\partial\varepsilon B}{\partial t} + rac{\partial\varepsilon BU}{\partial x} + rac{\partial\varepsilon BW}{\partial z} - rac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_\varepsilon} rac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial z} ight) - rac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_\varepsilon} rac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial x} ight) = B\left(C_{\varepsilon 1} rac{\varepsilon}{k}P - C_{\varepsilon 2} rac{\varepsilon^2}{k} + P_\varepsilon ight) ag{2-86} \] \[ rac{\partial kB}{\partial t} + rac{\partial kBU}{\partial x} + rac{\partial kBW}{\partial z} - rac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_k} rac{\partial k}{\partial z} ight) - rac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_k} rac{\partial k}{\partial x} ight) = B(P + G - \varepsilon + P_k) ag{2-87} \]

where \(C_\mu\) is an empirical constant and:

  • \(P = u_t\left( rac{\partial U}{\partial z} ight)^2\) (production)
  • \(G = - rac{ u_t}{\sigma_t}N^2\) (buoyancy)
  • \(P_k = rac{C_f |u^3|}{0.5B}\) (production term from boundary friction)
  • \(P_\varepsilon = rac{10 C_f^{1.25} u^4}{(0.5B)^2}\) (production term from boundary friction)
  • Brunt-Vaisala frequency \(N = \sqrt{- rac{g}{ ho} rac{d ho}{dz}}\)

\(B\) is the width, \(U\) and \(W\) are the advective velocities in x and z respectively, and other terms are empirical constants.

Typical values of the above model constants that have been used in other studies are:

\(C_\mu\) \(C_{\varepsilon 1}\) \(C_{\varepsilon 2}\) \(\sigma_k\) \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) 0.09 1.44 1.92 1.0 1.3

Turbulent Prandtl/Schmidt number, \(\sigma_t\) = 1.0.

The friction coefficient \(C_f\) is defined as:

\[ C_f = rac{g}{C^2} = rac{gn^2}{R_h^{1/3}} ag{2-95} \]

where \(g\) is gravitational acceleration, \(C\) is a Chezy friction factor, \(n\) is a Manning's friction factor, and \(R_h\) is the hydraulic radius.

The solution of the above equations for \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) uses a split solution technique: explicit horizontal and source-sink term solution followed by an implicit vertical solution. A description of the solution algorithm is based on Gould (2006).

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
The current algorithm is based on the laterally averaged k-ε turbulence model equations shown below:

\[ u_t = C_\mu rac{k^2}{\varepsilon} ag{2-88} \] \[ rac{\partial kB}{\partial t} + rac{\partial(kUB)}{\partial x} + rac{\partial(kWB)}{\partial z} - rac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_k} rac{\partial k}{\partial z} ight) = B(P + G - \varepsilon + P_k) ag{2-89} \] \[ rac{\partial\varepsilon B}{\partial t} + rac{\partial(\varepsilon UB)}{\partial x} + rac{\partial(\varepsilon WB)}{\partial z} - rac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(B rac{ u_t}{\sigma_\varepsilon} rac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial z} ight) = B\left(C_{\varepsilon 1} rac{\varepsilon}{k}P - C_{\varepsilon 2} rac{\varepsilon^2}{k} + P_\varepsilon ight) ag{2-90} \]

where \( u_t\), \(k\), and \(\varepsilon\) are the eddy viscosity, turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent dissipation. \(P\) is the production term and is calculated using:

\[ P = u_t\left( rac{\partial U}{\partial z} ight)^2 ag{2-91} \]

and \(G\) is the buoyancy term:

\[ G = - rac{ u_t}{\sigma_t}N^2 ag{2-92} \]

The production of turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent dissipation from boundary friction are represented by the terms \(P_k\) and \(P_\varepsilon\).

The equations above are solved using a split solution technique similar to the horizontal momentum equation in CE-QUAL-W2. Two methods are available:

  1. The vertical transport term is solved using an explicit finite difference along with the horizontal transport term.
  2. The vertical transport term is integrated into a fully implicit finite difference.

Both methods are based on the solutions developed by Wells (2001). The computational grid used in these calculations is shown in Figure 28.

docs.title: Boundary and Initial Conditions for k-ε Model
docs.text:
To apply this algorithm to CE-QUAL-W2 hydraulic problems, boundary conditions for the bed, free surface, inlet, and outlet, as well as initial conditions, must be specified.

At the bed, steep gradients of turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent dissipation are present in the viscous sublayer. To avoid this problem, an empirical law can be used to construct a simple wall function. The largest assumption is that the flow parallel to the wall obeys the law of the wall:

\[ rac{U}{U_*} = rac{1}{\kappa}\ln\left(E rac{yU_*}{ u} ight) ag{2-130} \]

where \(U_*\) is the bed friction velocity, \(\kappa\) is the von Karman constant, \(y\) is the distance of the grid point from the bed, \(E\) is the roughness coefficient and \( u\) is the kinematic viscosity.

The boundary condition for turbulent kinetic energy at the first grid point is (Rodi, 1993):

\[ k = rac{U_*^2}{\sqrt{C_\mu}} ag{2-132} \]

The boundary condition for turbulent dissipation is:

\[ \varepsilon = rac{U_*^3}{\kappa y} ag{2-133} \]

For hydraulically smooth beds the roughness coefficient \(E\) is set to 9.535 (Ferziger and Peric, 2002). For rough boundaries a smaller value of \(E\) is used. Two options are available in the current algorithm for specifying the roughness coefficient: a uniform constant value applied to all segments, or a value calculated based on the Manning's coefficients specified in the bathymetry file.

For the free surface boundary conditions, the following apply:

\[ rac{\partial k}{\partial y} = 0 ag{2-138} \] \[ \varepsilon = rac{k^{3/2}}{aH} ag{2-139} \]

where \(a\) is an empirical constant and \(H\) is the depth of the shear layer (channel depth). The coefficient \(a\) was originally set to a value of 0.18 by Celik and Rodi (1984) and then later changed to a value of 0.43 by Celik and Rodi (1988).

The initial conditions and inlet boundary conditions are specified by setting the eddy viscosity, turbulent kinetic energy, and turbulent dissipation terms to the following values:

  • \( u_t = 1.4 imes 10^{-6}\)
  • \(k = 1.25 imes 10^{-7}\)
  • \(\varepsilon = 1.0 imes 10^{-9}\)

The outlet values of turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent dissipation are determined using a zero-gradient approach:

\[ rac{\partial k}{\partial x} = 0, \quad rac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial x} = 0 \]

This is done by setting the value of turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent dissipation at the outlet cell equal to the value of the cell in the upstream segment.

docs.title: Effect of Vertical Layer Numbers on Vertical Turbulence
docs.text:
In contrast to other riverine models that assume vertically well-mixed systems, CE-QUAL-W2 accounts for the vertical variation of velocity in a riverine reach. Even though there is an added computational burden of computing the 2D velocity profile, the advantage of making this computation is that the friction factor (Manning's or Chezy) for a segment can be flow or stage invariant depending on the number of vertical layers schematized.

Many one-dimensional (1D) hydraulic flow models, such as CE-QUAL-RIV1 and UNET (Barkau, 1997), allow the user to specify how Manning's friction factor changes with depth. The Manning's friction factor, \(n\), has been thought to vary as a function of depth, Reynolds number, and roughness factor or scale of bed grain size (Ugarte and Madrid, 1994; Soong et al., 1995).

However, in a two-dimensional, longitudinal-vertical river model, Manning's friction factor does not have to vary with stage to produce the effect that apparent friction decreases as river stage increases. The water surface setup changes significantly with the number of layers. In general, water surface slope increases as the number of computational layers decreases, because the average eddy viscosity in the water column increases with fewer layers. At the limit of a one-layer system, the average vertical eddy viscosity is infinite.

The model allows choosing between six different vertical eddy viscosity formulations. These formulations are shown in Table 2. Typical variation of these formulations is shown in Figure 24 for Manning's friction factor for an open-channel, non-stratified flow regime as compared to theory of steady, uniform channel flow.

The number of vertical layers significantly affects model predictions. For example, Figure 32 shows a comparison of vertical velocity profiles from a model with one, three, and seven vertical layers using the parabolic eddy viscosity model.

docs.title: Longitudinal Shear Stress
docs.text:
The longitudinal turbulent shear stress is defined as:

\[ \frac{\tau_{xx}}{\rho} = \nu_t\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = A_x\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} \tag{2-142} \]

where \(A_x = \nu_t\) = longitudinal eddy viscosity.

\(A_x\) is a user-defined constant or it can be set to scale with the average longitudinal velocity. This turbulence closure approximation is termed a zero-order closure model since no further equations are necessary to solve for the transmission of shear stress within the fluid.

This term is usually of very low magnitude except in areas near boundaries such as at a dam face where the longitudinal velocity goes to zero.

The equation for computing \(A_x\) is:

\[ A_x = \alpha\bar{U}\Delta z \]

where α is a user input value, \(U\) with double bars are the time-averaged, lateral averaged longitudinal velocity at a segment and layer.

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
The user can specify a pipe or culvert between model segments (Berger and Wells, 1999) using a 1D, unsteady hydraulic model that computes the flow between the two linked segments. The model computes the selective withdrawal outflow from the upstream segment. The user specifies whether the inflow to the downstream segment is mixed over the depth, placed at the depth determined from inflow density, or distributed between an upper and lower elevation.

This model is only appropriate for simple piping systems that are not suddenly under a large hydraulic head. The governing equations for computing the flow and the numerical solution technique are shown below.

The governing equations used to predict flow through culverts are the 1D, time-dependent conservation of momentum and continuity equations (Yen, 1973):

\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + g\cos\varphi\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - g(S_o - S_f - S_m) = 0 \tag{2-143} \] \[ \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \frac{A}{T}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0 \tag{2-144} \]

where:

  • \(u\) = velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(t\) = time, s
  • \(h\) = piezometric head, m
  • \(g\) = gravitational acceleration, m s⁻²
  • \(x\) = distance along axis of culvert, m
  • \(A\) = cross-sectional area of culvert filled with water, m²
  • \(T\) = width of water level surface, m
  • \(\varphi\) = angle between culvert axis and horizontal
  • \(S_o\) = culvert slope
  • \(S_f\) = friction slope
  • \(S_m\) = minor loss slope

The friction slope \(S_f\) is estimated using the Manning formula:

\[ S_f = \frac{n^2}{R^{4/3}}u|u| \tag{2-145} \]

Minor losses due to entrance configuration, gates, valves, and corners are accounted for in the minor loss term \(S_m\):

\[ S_m = k\frac{u|u|}{2g}\frac{1}{L} \tag{2-146} \]

where:

  • \(k\) = sum of minor loss coefficients
  • \(L\) = length

Pressurized or full culvert flow is modeled using a fictitious water surface width called a Preissmann slot (Yen, 1986). If the culvert is full, the surface width \(T\) is zero and the governing equations become singular. The Preissmann slot avoids switching between the open channel and pressurized flow equations. A top width of 0.5% of the diameter is assumed for culverts flowing full.

The advantages of using a Preissmann slot are (Yen, 1986):

  1. Uses only Saint-Venant equations and avoids switching between the surcharge equation and open-channel flow equations
  2. No need to define surcharge criteria
  3. Not necessary to keep inventory of the pipes that are surcharged at different times
  4. Permits the flow transition to progress computationally reach by reach in a sewer
  5. Requires few additional assumptions than the standard approach to achieve numerical stability
  6. Simpler to program

The disadvantages are:

  1. Introduces a potential accuracy problem in the mass and momentum balance of the flow if the slot is too wide, and stability problems if it is too narrow
  2. Requires computation of two equations (continuity and momentum) for each of the reaches of the sewer when the sewer is full surcharged
  3. Hypothetical rather than real

The boundary condition used for solving the governing equations is the head or water level at each end of the culvert. However, if the water level at the downstream end of the culvert is less than the critical depth, the critical depth is used. Momentum is not transferred between model segments and the culverts. Initial conditions are the calculated velocities and heads at the previous time step.

docs.title: Internal Weirs
docs.text: The model can be used to set internal weirs at specified cell locations. The user specifies the location of the internal weir by providing a segment and layer number. The "weir" effectively acts as a barrier to flow and diffusion of mass/heat across the width of the waterbody. This can be used to simulate submerged and curtain weirs within a waterbody.

docs.title: Water Level Control or Pumps
docs.text:
In many reservoir systems, outflows are controlled by water levels. A water level control or pump algorithm allows the user to specify the upstream and downstream segments for water transfer at a given flow rate based on the water level at the upstream segment. This is essentially a pump based on a float controller.

Reverse flow is not allowed. The withdrawal is treated as a lateral selective withdrawal, and the receiving segment is treated as a tributary inflow.

docs.title: Outlet Structures
docs.text:
Outflows through hydraulic structures can either be specified or computed by the model based on user-supplied rating curves.

The UNET model (Hydrologic Engineering Center [HEC], 1997a), a one-dimensional unsteady hydraulic model, formally accounts for spillway flow from weirs and spillways. For free or submerged flow from a spillway with a radial gate, UNET uses a general equation of the form:

\[ Q_{sp} = CWA^\alpha B^\beta H^\eta \tag{2-149} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\beta\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\eta\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(Q_{sp}\) = flow rate, m³ s⁻¹
  • \(A\) = trunnion height, m
  • \(B\) = gate opening, m
  • \(C\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(W\) = gate width, m

and

\[ H = Z_u - KZ_d - (1-K)Z_{sp} \tag{2-150} \]

where:

  • \(Z_u\) = headwater elevation
  • \(Z_d\) = tailwater elevation
  • \(K\) = 1 for submerged flow and 0 for free flow
  • \(Z_{sp}\) = spillway elevation

Submergence is defined as:

\[ \frac{Z_d - Z_{sp}}{Z_u - Z_{sp}} > \frac{2}{3} \tag{2-151} \]

Note that weir flow is assumed to occur whenever \(B = 0.8H\) and is computed as:

\[ Q_{weir} = C_w FW\left((1-K)Z_u + KZ_d - Z_{sp}\right)H^{1/2} \tag{2-152} \]

where:

  • \(C_w\) = weir coefficient
  • \(F = 3\left(1-\frac{|Z_d-Z_{sp}|}{|Z_u-Z_{sp}|}\right)\) when \(K = 1\)
  • \(F = 1\) when \(K = 0\)

For a concrete spillway, HEC (1997a) suggests using a weir coefficient value of 4. Note that the above two equations are considered equivalent whenever \(B = 0.8H\).

HEC-RAS (Hydrologic Engineering Center River Analysis System), a one-dimensional, steady-state hydraulic model (HEC, 1997b), includes the ability to model flow over spillways including tainter and sluice gates, broad-crested weirs, and an ogee crest. A summary of the equations used by HEC-RAS is shown in Table 4.

docs.title: Spillways/Weirs
docs.text:
Analysis of flow over weirs has been studied extensively. Martin and McCutcheon (1999) show that a typical relationship between the pool depth and flow over a weir is:

\[ Q = C_e W_c h_w^\eta \tag{2-153} \]

where \(C_e\) and \(\eta\) are empirical coefficients, \(W_c\) is the length of the weir crest, and \(h_w\) is the height of the pool above the weir crest. Theoretical calculations of steady-state flow over a weir can be complex depending on whether the weirs are sharp-crested, broad-crested, V-notched, rectangular, Cipolletti, parabolic, or some other type.

Since all weirs in practice are calibrated and a head discharge relationship is usually determined, the flow versus head relationship is used rather than an equation from Table 5. The user must then analyze the weir or spillway and input a relationship based on the weir or spillway geometry. The model accepts equations in the form of a power function for freely flowing conditions:

\[ Q = \alpha_1\Delta h^{\beta_1} \tag{A-2-154} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha_1\) = empirical parameter
  • \(\beta_1\) = empirical parameter
  • \(\Delta h = Z_u - Z_{sp}\)
  • \(Z_u\) = upstream head
  • \(Z_{sp}\) = spillway crest elevation

and for submerged conditions:

\[ Q = \alpha_2\Delta h^{\beta_2} \tag{A-2-155} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha_2\) = empirical parameter
  • \(\beta_2\) = empirical parameter
  • \(\Delta h = Z_u - Z_d\)
  • \(Z_u\) = upstream head
  • \(Z_d\) = downstream head

Submerged conditions are defined when the tailwater depth over the upstream energy head (static head and velocity head) is greater than 0.67 (HEC, 1997b). Negative flow rates are possible using the second equation whenever \(Z_d > Z_u\); however, use these results with caution since rating curves are rarely calibrated for reverse flow over a spillway.

Warning

Ensure a smooth transition between submerged and free flowing conditions by proper choice of model coefficients.

For a smooth transition, the two flows must be equal at the transition point. Using:

\[ H_2 - H_{weir} = 0.67\left(\Delta h_1 + \frac{u^2}{2g}\right) \approx 0.67(H_1 - H_{weir}) \tag{2-156} \]

and substituting the rating curves for free flow and submerged conditions and solving for \(\alpha_2\) results in:

\[ \alpha_2 = \frac{\alpha_1(H_1-H_{weir})^{\beta_1-\beta_2}}{(0.33)^{\beta_2}} \tag{2-157} \]

In many cases a weir can be set as the downstream boundary condition of a river. In CE-QUAL-W2, the user can specify the weir crest as the channel bottom elevation, such that the weir equation is of the form:

\[ Q = \alpha_1 H^{\beta_1} \tag{2-158} \]

where \(H\) is the depth of the water at the weir. Setting this in the form of a stage-discharge relationship:

\[ H = aQ^b = \left(\frac{Q}{\alpha_1}\right)^{1/\beta_1} \tag{2-159} \]

Then the a and b coefficients become:

\[ a = \left(\frac{1}{\alpha_1}\right)^{1/\beta_1} \tag{2-161} \] \[ b = \frac{1}{\beta_1} \tag{2-162} \]

or vice versa:

\[ \alpha_1 = a^{-\beta_1} \tag{2-163} \] \[ \beta_1 = \frac{1}{b} \tag{2-164} \]

This allows the user to set a weir-rating curve that reproduces the stage discharge relationship at a downstream boundary.

A dynamic weir or spillway crest elevation can also be used to simulate dynamic raising of flashboards. These are designated in the model as gates.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
For a gated structure or sluice gate, a more complex rating curve is required based on the opening and the head difference between the upstream and downstream condition (the spillway crest if free flow and the tailwater elevation if submerged flow).

The following equation is used for freely flowing conditions:

\[ Q = \alpha_1\Delta h^{\beta_1}B^{\gamma_1} \tag{2-165} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha_1\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\beta_1\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\gamma_1\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\Delta h = Z_u - Z_{sp}\)
  • \(Z_u\) = upstream head
  • \(Z_{sp}\) = spillway crest elevation

and the following equation is used for submerged flow:

\[ Q = \alpha_2\Delta h^{\beta_2}B^{\gamma_2} \tag{2-166} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha_2\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\beta_2\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\gamma_2\) = empirical coefficient
  • \(\Delta h = Z_u - Z_d\)
  • \(Z_d\) = downstream head
  • \(B\) = gate opening, m

In defining these parameters, the user also has to generate a time series file with the gate opening in m where a gate opening of 0 m is closed. Whenever the gate opening is equal to or greater than \(0.8\Delta h\), a weir equation is used with no functional dependency on the gate opening. In this case, a rating curve must be supplied when the gate acts like a weir.

In some reservoir systems, an outlet valve is connected to the reservoir and a head-discharge relationship is used based on the gate opening or number of gate turns. In this case, the outlet level is usually at a different elevation than the withdrawal elevation. The above gate formulation can still be used if no reverse flow occurs through the needle valve.

The user can insert weirs and/or spillways, specify connectivity to other model segments, and provide rating curve parameters for each structure. The model treats each spillway, weir, or gate as a selective withdrawal outflow and uses the selective withdrawal algorithm to determine flow from each vertical layer adjacent to the structure.

Inflows from hydraulic control structures are treated as tributary inflows. The user must specify whether the inflow is placed according to density, distributed equally between all vertical layers, or distributed between a given elevation range.

Weir equations are used when gates are open and the open gate does not interfere with the flow (when \(B \ge 0.8\Delta h\)).

Gates can also be used to move flows around to different parts of the model domain, including different branches. In that case the specification of gate openings is interpreted as specification of flow rates.

docs.title: Branch Momentum Exchange
docs.text:
Starting with CE-QUAL-W2 Version 3, CE-QUAL-W2 conserves longitudinal momentum at branch intersections. The vector component of velocity in the x-direction of the main channel, \(U_x\), can be computed from the channel orientations. The x-direction component is \(U_x = U\cos\beta\) where \(U\) is the longitudinal velocity of the tributary at the downstream segment that intersects the main branch and \(\beta\) is the difference in the angle between the main stem and tributary segments.

The conservation of momentum about a control volume (the main stem segment) would result in an additional source of momentum. Lai (1986) shows that the correction to the x-momentum equation would be:

\[ qBU_x \tag{2-167} \]

where \(q\) = lateral inflow per unit length.

This arises from re-deriving the momentum equations and assuming that all the fluid entering the segment is moving at the velocity \(U_x\). The correction to the x-momentum equation is:

\[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z} = gB\sin\alpha + g\cos\alpha B\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho}\int_{\eta}^{z}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial x}\,dz + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial B\tau_{xz}}{\partial z} + qBU_x \tag{2-168} \]

docs.title: Lateral Inflows
docs.text:
Wells (1997) proposed accounting for the cross-shear as a result of the y component of the velocity of a side branch in the computation of the vertical eddy viscosity. This was implemented by increasing the cross-shear velocity gradient. In Version 2, wind shear across the lateral axis of a segment also increased the vertical mixing by affecting the computation of \(A_z\). Analogous to wind shear, an additional side shear is included in the calculation of the vertical eddy viscosity:

\[ A_z = \kappa\left(\frac{l^2}{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\tau_{wy}e^{-2kz}+\tau_{trib}}{\rho A_z}\right)^2}\;e^{-CRi} \tag{2-169} \]

where:

  • \(\tau_{trib} \cong \rho\frac{f_i}{8}U_y^2\)
  • \(f_i\) = interfacial friction factor, \(\approx 0.01\)
  • \(U_y = \frac{\sum Q_{in_y}}{\Delta z \Delta x}\)
  • \(\sum Q_{in_y} = [U_{br}\Delta z B] + \left[\sum Q_{trib}\right]\)
  • \(U_{br} = U_{br}\sin(\Theta_{main}-\Theta_{branch})\)
  • \(\Delta z\) = inflow cell layer height
  • \(B\) = inflow cell width
  • \(\Delta x\) = inflow cell segment length
  • \(Q_{trib}\) = tributary flow rate assumed to be at right angles to the main channel

This side shear effect is only computed when the vertical mixing algorithm chosen by the user is W2 or W2N.

docs.title: Density
docs.text:
Accurate hydrodynamic calculations require accurate water densities. Water densities are affected by variations in temperature and solids concentrations given by:

\[ \rho = \rho_T + \Delta\rho_S \tag{2-170} \]

where:

  • \(\rho\) = density, kg m⁻³
  • \(\rho_T\) = water density as a function of temperature, kg m⁻³
  • \(\Delta\rho_S\) = density increment due to solids, kg m⁻³

A variety of formulations has been proposed to describe water density variations due to temperatures. The following relationship is used in the model (Gill, 1982):

\[ \rho_{T_w} = 999.842594 + 6.793952 \times 10^{-2}T_w - 9.095290 \times 10^{-3}T_w^2 + 1.001685 \times 10^{-4}T_w^3 - 1.120083 \times 10^{-6}T_w^4 + 6.536332 \times 10^{-9}T_w^5 \tag{2-171} \]

Suspended and dissolved solids also affect density. For most applications, dissolved solids are represented as total dissolved solids (TDS). For estuarine applications, specify salinity instead. The choice is controlled by the variable [WTYPE].

Density effects due to TDS are given by Ford and Johnson (1983):

\[ \Delta\rho_{TDS} = (8.221 \times 10^{-4} - 3.87 \times 10^{-6}T_w + 4.99 \times 10^{-8}T_w^2)\Phi_{TDS} \tag{2-172} \]

where \(\Phi_{TDS}\) = total dissolved solids (TDS) concentration, g m⁻³.

And for salinity (Gill, 1982):

\[ \Delta\rho_{sal} = (0.824493 - 4.0899 \times 10^{-3}T_w + 7.6438 \times 10^{-5}T_w^2 - 8.2467 \times 10^{-7}T_w^3 + 5.3875 \times 10^{-9}T_w^4)\Phi_{sal} + (-5.72466 \times 10^{-3} + 1.0227 \times 10^{-4}T_w - 1.6546 \times 10^{-6}T_w^2)\Phi_{sal}^{1.5} + 4.8314 \times 10^{-4}\Phi_{sal}^2 \tag{2-173} \]

where \(\Phi_{sal}\) = salinity, kg m⁻³.

The suspended solids effects are given by Ford and Johnson (1983):

\[ \Delta\rho_{SS} = \Phi_{SS}\left(1 - \frac{1}{SG}\right) \times 10^{-3} \tag{2-174} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{SS}\) = suspended solids concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(SG\) = specific gravity of suspended solids

Assuming a specific gravity of 2.65, the above relationship is simplified to:

\[ \Delta\rho_{SS} = 0.00062\Phi_{SS} \tag{2-175} \]

The total effect of solids is then:

\[ \Delta\rho_S = (\Delta\rho_{sal} \text{ or } \Delta\rho_{TDS}) + \Delta\rho_{SS} \tag{2-176} \]

docs.title: Selective Withdrawal
docs.text:
To model the complex outlet hydraulics in a reservoir, selective withdrawal algorithms are used (Brooks and Koh, 1969; Davis et al., 1987). These allow the computation of flow from multiple vertical layers without solving the full vertical momentum equation.

Selective withdrawal is applied to all structure outflows. Layer locations and outflows at each layer are calculated based on the total outflow [QOUT], structure type [SINKC], elevation [ESTR], and computed upstream density gradients. The selective withdrawal computation determines vertical withdrawal zone limits and outflows, and sums the outflows for multiple structures. All outflows (including withdrawals and hydraulic structures) use selective withdrawal theory to compute the withdrawal envelope.

Outflow distribution is calculated in the subroutine SELECTIVE_WITHDRAWAL. This routine first calculates limits of withdrawal based on either a user-specified point or line sink approximation for outlet geometry [SINKC]. The empirical expression for point sink withdrawal limits is:

\[ d = \left(\frac{c_{bi}Q}{N}\right)^{0.33} \tag{2-177} \]

and for a line sink:

\[ d = \left(\frac{2c_{bi}q}{N}\right)^{0.5} \tag{2-178} \]

where:

  • \(d\) = withdrawal zone half height, m
  • \(Q\) = total outflow, m³ s⁻¹
  • \(N\) = internal buoyancy frequency, Hz, \(N = \sqrt{-\frac{g}{\rho}\frac{d\rho}{dz}}\)
  • \(q\) = outflow per unit width, m² s⁻¹, q=Q/W where W is the outlet width of the line sink
  • \(c_{bi}\) = boundary interference coefficient

The point sink approximation assumes approach flow is radial both longitudinally and vertically while the line sink approximation assumes flow approaches the outlet radially in the vertical. The boundary interference coefficient is two near a physical boundary and one elsewhere.

Velocities are determined using a quadratic shape function:

\[ V_k = 1 - \left[\frac{(\rho_k - \rho_o)}{(\rho_l - \rho_o)}\right]^2 \tag{2-179} \]

where:

  • \(V_k\) = normalized velocity in layer \(k\)
  • \(\rho_k\) = density in layer \(k\), kg m⁻³
  • \(\rho_o\) = density in the outlet layer, kg m⁻³
  • \(\rho_l\) = density of the withdrawal limit layer, kg m⁻³

The shape function generates a maximum velocity at the outlet level with velocities approaching zero at withdrawal limits. During non-stratified periods, outflow from top to bottom is uniform. Uniform flows also result from large outflows during periods of mild stratification. As stratification develops, withdrawal limits decrease and outflow is weighted towards the outlet elevation.

Withdrawal limits can be varied by specifying a line sink and changing the effective width. Small outlet widths result in nearly uniform outflows, while large widths limit outflows to the outlet layer.

docs.title: Sediment Resuspension
docs.text:
This algorithm is based on work by Kang et al. (1982), where bottom shear stress is computed from wind speed, wind fetch, and depth. Wind blowing across a water surface creates wind waves with orbital motion that decays with depth. The user inputs a critical shear stress for particle detachment; if this threshold is exceeded, particles are resuspended.

The approach of Kang et al. (1982) consists of the following steps:

  1. Computation of the wave height, \(H_s\) in m:
\[ H_s = \frac{W^2}{g}0.283\tanh\left[0.53\left(\frac{gH}{W^2}\right)^{0.75}\right]\tanh\left[\frac{0.0125\left(\frac{gF}{W^2}\right)^{0.42}}{\tanh\left[0.53\left(\frac{gH}{W^2}\right)^{0.75}\right]}\right] \tag{2-180} \] 
where $W$ is the wind velocity (m s⁻¹), $F$ is the fetch (m), $H$ is the mean depth (m).
  1. Computation of wave period, \(T_s\) in s:
\[ T_s = \frac{2\pi W}{g}1.2\tanh\left[0.833\left(\frac{gH}{W^2}\right)^{0.375}\right]\tanh\left[\frac{0.077\left(\frac{gF}{W^2}\right)^{0.25}}{\tanh\left[0.833\left(\frac{gH}{W^2}\right)^{0.375}\right]}\right] \tag{2-181} \]
  1. Computation of the wavelength, \(L\) in m, iteratively from the following equation:
\[ L = \frac{gT_s^2}{2\pi}\tanh\left[\frac{2\pi H}{L}\right] \tag{2-182} \]
  1. Computation of the orbital velocity, \(\tilde{U}\) in cm s⁻¹:
\[ \tilde{U} = \frac{\pi H_s}{T_s}\frac{100}{\sinh(2\pi H/L)} \tag{2-183} \]
  1. Computation of bottom shear stress, \(\tau\) in dynes cm⁻²:
\[ \tau = 0.003\tilde{U}^2 \tag{2-184} \]
  1. Computation of actual bottom scour rate of suspended solids, \(\varepsilon\) in g m⁻²:
\[ \varepsilon = 0 \quad \tau \le \tau_c \tag{2-185} \] \[ \varepsilon = \frac{\alpha_o}{\tau_d^4}(\tau - \tau_c)^3 \quad \tau > \tau_c \tag{2-186} \] 
where $\alpha_o$ is an empirical constant (0.008), $\tau_d$ = 7, and $\tau_c$ is the user-defined critical shear stress in dynes cm⁻².

Resuspension is assumed to occur only during the first hour after wind shear exceeds the critical shear stress. The rate of resuspension, \(E\) in g m⁻² hr⁻¹, is:

\[ E = \frac{\varepsilon}{1hr} \]

for the first hour and zero thereafter. The resulting concentration of suspended solids in the water column, \(c\) in mg/L, if distributed evenly over the entire volume is:

\[ c = \frac{10000\varepsilon A_{bottom}}{V} = \frac{10000\varepsilon}{H} \]

where \(A_{bottom}\) is the surface area of the bottom and \(V\) is the volume of the water column above the bottom (=\(HA_{bottom}\)). Chapra (1997) also uses this approach and provides an example calculation.

docs.title: Particle Tracking Algorithm
docs.text: The original particle tracking algorithm in CE-QUAL-W2 was developed by Goodwin et al. (2001) for use in a smart-particle tracking algorithm that predicts the movement of fish in a southern reservoir in the United States. This chapter describes the mathematical formulation for tracking discrete particles through the CE-QUAL-W2 computational grid.

docs.title: Algorithm Description
docs.text: The particle-tracking algorithm was developed by Chapman et al. (1994) to predict transport and fate of floatables and suspended and dissolved materials in three dimensions. The algorithm was simplified for use in CE-QUAL-W2 by removing portions of the model relating to surface transport of floatables and suspended and dissolved materials. Transport equations for lateral movement were also removed because CE-QUAL-W2 computes forcing functions only in the longitudinal and vertical directions.

docs.title: Advective Transport Equations
docs.text:
The following equations are used for particle tracking in CE-QUAL-W2 based on velocity:

\[ X^{t+1} = X^{t} + U^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t}) \cdot \Delta t \tag{3-1} \] \[ Z^{t+1} = Z^{t} + W^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t}) \cdot \Delta t \tag{3-2} \]

docs.title: Variable Definitions
docs.text:
The variables in the transport equations are defined as follows:

Variable Definition Node(k,i) Node above, upstream, and closest to the particle's position, defined as the upper-left node of the rectangular cell formed by intersection of vertical layer k and longitudinal segment i \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\) Longitudinal position of Node(k,i) (m) \(\Delta x\) Offset (downstream) from Node(k,i) to the particle's position (m) \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\) Vertical position of Node(k,i) (m) \(\Delta z\) Offset (below) from Node(k,i) to the particle's position (m) \(X^{t}\) Longitudinal position of particle at time \(t\) (m); defined as \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta x\) at time \(t\) \(Z^{t}\) Vertical position of particle at time \(t\) (m); defined as \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta z\) at time \(t\) \(X^{t+1}\) Longitudinal position of particle at time \(t+1\) (m) \(Z^{t+1}\) Vertical position of particle at time \(t+1\) (m) \(U^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t})\) Interpolated horizontal flow velocity (m/s) at location \((Z^{t}, X^{t})\) \(W^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t})\) Interpolated vertical flow velocity (m/s) at location \((Z^{t}, X^{t})\) \(\Delta t\) Time interval between time \(t\) and time \(t+1\) (seconds)

docs.title: Boundary Checks
docs.text:
After \(X^{t+1}\) and \(Z^{t+1}\) are calculated, boundary checks determine whether the particle's new position exceeds the longitudinal or vertical boundaries of the cell containing \(X^{t}\) and \(Z^{t}\), or any system boundary. If the new position exceeds the boundaries of the previous cell, an algorithm identifies the appropriate cell in which to place the particle. Once the correct cell is found, the values of k, i, Node(k,i), \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\), \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\), \(\Delta x\), and \(\Delta z\) are updated for the particle at \(t+1\) and stored.

Since the displacement of a particle is proportional to the time step used, the displacement calculated in Equations 3-1 and 3-2 could position the particle outside system boundaries. To correct for this, the model places a particle near the boundary at a user-specified distance if \(X^{t+1}\) or \(Z^{t+1}\) exceeds the system boundaries.

docs.title: Turbulent Diffusion
docs.text:
In addition to advective transport, a random movement is added to represent the effects of turbulence. The magnitude of the random movement is proportional to the intensity of turbulence in the system. Following Dunsbergen and Stalling (1993) and Chapman et al. (1994), the transport in x and z including both advection and random turbulent transport is:

\[ X^{t+1} = X^{t} + U \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_x \Delta t} \tag{3-3} \] \[ Z^{t+1} = Z^{t} + W \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_z \Delta t} \tag{3-4} \]

where:

  • \(R\) = a random number having a uniform distribution with zero mean and unit variance
  • \(D_x\) = longitudinal mass/heat dispersion coefficient
  • \(D_z\) = vertical mass/heat dispersion coefficient

The use of the uniform distribution rather than a Gaussian distribution saves computational time and does not affect the resulting random distribution (Hathhorn, 1997).

docs.title: Dispersion Coefficient Specification
docs.text:
The value of \(D_x\) is specified in the control file w2_con.npt, whereas \(D_z\) is computed by the turbulence closure model selected for the simulation (for example, setting [AZC] to TKE activates the k-ε turbulence model). A high value of \(D_x\) can produce excessive random longitudinal movement. In all cases, the maximum displacement of a particle per time step is constrained by the grid cell height (\(\Delta z\)) and segment length (\(\Delta x\)).

High Dispersion Coefficient Values

Setting \(D_x\) to a high value can cause excessive random longitudinal movement of particles. The maximum particle displacement per time step is bounded by the grid cell dimensions (\(\Delta z\) and \(\Delta x\)).

docs.title: Lateral Transport
docs.text:
Particles also move in the lateral direction based on the following equation, assuming that the lateral dispersion coefficient is the same as the longitudinal coefficient:

\[ Y^{t+1} = Y^{t} + V \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_x \Delta t} \tag{3-5} \]

The value of \(V\) is based on any lateral inflows or outflows at a segment.

docs.title: Particle Location in the Grid
docs.text:
The location of each particle in the grid is identified by segment (I) and layer (K) indices as well as X, Y, and Z coordinates within each cell. The standard CE-QUAL-W2 sign convention is followed in this algorithm:

  • Longitudinal velocity: positive downstream (increasing segment number)
  • Vertical velocity: positive downward

Initial x, y, and z coordinates are specified for each particle released into a segment and layer. The user specifies x and z; y is set to the middle of the layer, that is, \(y = B/2\) where \(B\) is the layer width.

docs.title: Plan View Coordinates
docs.text:
Within a given layer K and segment I, the coordinate system for the plan view is defined as follows:

  • X-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the right (looking downstream) to DLX at the left, with DLX\(/2\) at the center.
  • Y-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the left bank (looking upstream) to \(B\) at the right bank, with \(B/2\) at the center.

docs.title: Side View Coordinates
docs.text:
Within a given layer K and segment I, the coordinate system for the side view is defined as follows:

  • Z-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the top of the layer to DZ at the bottom, with DZ\(/2\) at the midpoint.
  • Y-coordinate: Same convention as the plan view (0 to \(B\)).

docs.title: Lateral and Longitudinal Velocities
docs.text:
The velocity sign conventions within each cell are:

  • Longitudinal velocity: Positive in the downstream direction (toward segment I+1), negative in the upstream direction.
  • Lateral velocity: Positive to the right (looking downstream), negative to the left.
  • Withdrawals: Always assumed to be on the left-hand side (LHS) of the segment.
  • Side branches: Can connect on either the left-hand side (LHS) or right-hand side (RHS) of a segment.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapman, R.S., Johnson, B.H., and Vemulakonda, S.R. (1994). User's Guide for the Sigma Stretched Version of CH3D-WES; a Three-Dimensional Numerical Hydrodynamic, Salinity, and Temperature Model. Technical Report HL-96-21, U.S. Army Engineer Waterways Experiment Station, Vicksburg, MS.
  • Dunsbergen, D.W., and Stalling, G.S. (1993). The Application of a Particle Model to Coastal and Estuarine Problems. Delft University of Technology, Dept. of Civil Engineering, Delft, The Netherlands.
  • Goodwin, R.A., Nestler, J.M., Anderson, J.J., Weber, L.J., and Loucks, D.P. (2001). A New Tool to Forecast Fish Movement and Passage. Hydro Review, 25(4), 74--82.
  • Hathhorn, W.E. (1997). A Second Look at the Method of Random Walks. Stochastic Hydrology and Hydraulics, 11(4), 319--329.
  • Kang, S.W., Sheng, Y.P., and Lick, W. (1982). Wave Action and Bottom Shear Stresses in Lake Erie. Journal of Great Lakes Research, 8(3), 482--494.

docs.title: Temperature and Water Quality Modeling
docs.text: This chapter describes the theoretical basis for temperature and water quality modeling in CE-QUAL-W2. The model simulates temperature and an arbitrary number of water quality constituents using the turbulent advection-diffusion equation. Each constituent is subject to lateral and vertical transport as well as kinetic source and sink terms that represent biological, chemical, and physical transformations.

docs.title: Temperature and Water Quality Transport
docs.text:
The laterally averaged transport equation for a constituent concentration \(\Phi\) is:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UB\Phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(BD_x\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x}\right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(BD_z\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z}\right) = q_\Phi B + S_K B \]

where:

  • \(\Phi\) = laterally averaged constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(U\) = longitudinal, laterally averaged velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(W\) = vertical, laterally averaged velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(B\) = channel width, m
  • \(D_x\) = longitudinal temperature and constituent dispersion coefficient, m² s⁻¹
  • \(D_z\) = vertical temperature and constituent dispersion coefficient, m² s⁻¹
  • \(q_\Phi\) = lateral inflow or outflow mass flow rate of constituent per unit volume, g m⁻³ s⁻¹
  • \(S_K\) = kinetic source/sink term for constituent concentration, g m⁻³ s⁻¹

The left-hand side of the equation represents the time rate of change, longitudinal advection, vertical advection, longitudinal dispersion, and vertical dispersion. The right-hand side includes lateral sources/sinks and internal kinetic transformations.

docs.title: Determination of \(D_z\) and \(D_x\)
docs.text:
The vertical dispersion coefficient \(D_z\) is derived from the turbulence closure model described in Chapter 2. For temperature simulations, \(D_z\) is computed from the turbulent eddy viscosity and the turbulent Prandtl number.

The longitudinal dispersion coefficient \(D_x\) accounts for the effects of differential advection that are not resolved by the laterally averaged model. The user specifies \(D_x\) through the control file parameter [DX]. Typical values range from 0 to 100 m² s⁻¹, though in many applications \(D_x\) is set to zero because numerical dispersion from the transport algorithm often exceeds the physical longitudinal dispersion.

docs.title: Heat Exchange
docs.text:
Temperature is modeled as a constituent with kinetic source/sink terms representing surface heat exchange and sediment heat exchange. The surface heat exchange rate is computed as:

\[ S_T = \frac{H_{net}}{\rho C_p \Delta z} \]

where:

  • \(H_{net}\) = net heat flux at the water surface, W m⁻²
  • \(\rho\) = water density, kg m⁻³
  • \(C_p\) = specific heat of water, J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹
  • \(\Delta z\) = surface layer thickness, m

docs.title: Surface Heat Exchange
docs.text:
The net surface heat flux is the sum of several components:

\[ H_{net} = H_s + H_a + H_{sr} + H_{ar} + H_e + H_c + H_{br} \]

where:

  • \(H_s\) = incident short-wave solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(H_a\) = incident long-wave atmospheric radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(H_{sr}\) = reflected short-wave solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(H_{ar}\) = reflected long-wave atmospheric radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(H_e\) = evaporative heat loss, W m⁻²
  • \(H_c\) = conductive heat transfer, W m⁻²
  • \(H_{br}\) = back radiation (long-wave radiation emitted by the water surface), W m⁻²

The model provides two approaches for computing surface heat exchange:

  • Term-by-term (TERM): Each heat flux component is calculated individually from meteorological data. Set SLHTC to TERM.
  • Equilibrium temperature (ET): The net heat exchange is computed as a linearized function of the difference between the water surface temperature and an equilibrium temperature. Set SLHTC to ET.

docs.title: Evaporation Models
docs.text:
CE-QUAL-W2 includes multiple formulations for the wind speed function used in evaporative heat loss calculations. The evaporative heat loss is computed as:

\[ H_e = f(W)(e_s - e_a) \]

where:

  • \(f(W)\) = wind speed function, W m⁻² mmHg⁻¹
  • \(e_s\) = saturation vapor pressure at the water surface temperature, mmHg
  • \(e_a\) = vapor pressure of the overlying atmosphere, mmHg

The user selects the evaporation formulation through the control file. Several wind speed function formulations are available including those from Brady, Harbeck, and Ryan-Harleman, among others.

docs.title: Equilibrium Temperature
docs.text:
The equilibrium temperature approach computes the net heat flux as:

\[ H_{net} = K_{eq}(T_{eq} - T_s) \]

where:

  • \(K_{eq}\) = coefficient of surface heat exchange, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(T_{eq}\) = equilibrium temperature, °C
  • \(T_s\) = water surface temperature, °C

The equilibrium temperature is the temperature at which the net heat flux is zero. Both \(K_{eq}\) and \(T_{eq}\) are computed internally by the model from meteorological data.

docs.title: Sediment Heat Exchange
docs.text:
Sediment-water heat exchange is computed as:

\[ H_{sed} = K_{sed}(T_{sed} - T) \]

where:

  • \(K_{sed}\) = sediment-water heat exchange coefficient, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(T_{sed}\) = sediment temperature, °C
  • \(T\) = water temperature of the bottom layer, °C

The sediment temperature is specified by the user through the control file parameter [TSED].

docs.title: Dynamic Shading
docs.text: CE-QUAL-W2 includes algorithms for computing the reduction of incident solar radiation due to topographic and vegetative shading. These algorithms account for the solar position (altitude and azimuth), local topography, and riparian vegetation along the channel.

docs.title: Solar Altitude and Azimuth
docs.text:
The solar altitude angle \(\alpha_s\) and azimuth angle \(A_s\) are computed from standard astronomical relationships as functions of latitude, longitude, day of the year, and time of day.

The solar altitude is computed as:

\[ \sin(\alpha_s) = \sin(\phi)\sin(\delta) + \cos(\phi)\cos(\delta)\cos(h) \]

where:

  • \(\phi\) = latitude
  • \(\delta\) = solar declination
  • \(h\) = hour angle

docs.title: Topographic Shading
docs.text: Topographic shading occurs when surrounding terrain blocks direct solar radiation from reaching the water surface. For each model segment, the user specifies topographic shade angles for both the left and right banks. When the solar altitude is less than the topographic shade angle, direct solar radiation is blocked.

docs.title: Vegetative Shading
docs.text: Vegetative shading accounts for the attenuation of solar radiation by riparian vegetation. The model computes the fraction of the water surface that is shaded based on tree height, crown width, distance from the bank, and solar position.

docs.title: Data Requirements
docs.text:
Dynamic shading requires segment-specific data including:

  • Topographic shade angles (left and right bank)
  • Vegetation characteristics: tree height, crown width, distance from bank, and canopy density
  • Model segment orientation (azimuth)

These data are specified in the shade input file.

docs.title: Ice Cover
docs.text: CE-QUAL-W2 simulates ice formation, growth, and decay. The ice model accounts for heat exchange between the atmosphere and ice surface, solar radiation transmission through ice, and heat exchange at the ice-water interface.

docs.title: Initial Formation
docs.text: Ice begins to form when the surface water temperature drops below the freezing temperature. The initial ice thickness is computed from the heat balance at the water surface.

docs.title: Air-Ice Flux Boundary Condition
docs.text:
When ice is present, the surface heat exchange is computed between the atmosphere and the ice surface rather than the water surface. The heat flux through the ice is:

\[ H_{ice} = \frac{k_{ice}}{h_{ice}}(T_1 - T_{ice}) \]

where:

  • \(k_{ice}\) = thermal conductivity of ice, W m⁻¹ °C⁻¹
  • \(h_{ice}\) = ice thickness, m
  • \(T_1\) = temperature at the bottom of the ice, °C
  • \(T_{ice}\) = temperature at the top of the ice surface, °C

docs.title: Solar Radiation Under Ice
docs.text:
Solar radiation penetration through ice is attenuated exponentially:

\[ I(z) = (1 - \alpha_{ice})I_0 e^{-\lambda_{ice} h_{ice}} \]

where:

  • \(\alpha_{ice}\) = ice albedo
  • \(I_0\) = incident solar radiation at the ice surface, W m⁻²
  • \(\lambda_{ice}\) = extinction coefficient for ice, m⁻¹
  • \(h_{ice}\) = ice thickness, m

docs.title: Ice Melt
docs.text: Ice melts when the heat flux from the water to the ice exceeds the heat flux from the ice to the atmosphere. Both surface melting (due to atmospheric heat flux) and bottom melting (due to water-to-ice heat flux) are computed.

docs.title: Ice-Water Flux Boundary Condition
docs.text:
The heat exchange at the ice-water interface is computed using a bulk transfer coefficient:

\[ H_{iw} = C_{iw}\rho C_p(T_w - T_f) \]

where:

  • \(C_{iw}\) = ice-water heat exchange coefficient, m s⁻¹
  • \(T_w\) = water temperature below the ice, °C
  • \(T_f\) = freezing temperature, °C

docs.title: Freezing Temperature
docs.text: The freezing temperature depends on total dissolved solids (TDS) or salinity. For freshwater, the freezing temperature is approximately 0 °C. For saline water, the freezing temperature decreases with increasing salinity.

docs.title: Gain or Loss of Water
docs.text: When ice forms, water is removed from the computational domain. When ice melts, water (at the freezing temperature) is returned to the surface layer. The model accounts for these changes in water volume.

docs.title: Overview of Kinetic Source/Sink Term
docs.text:
The kinetic source/sink term \(S_K\) in the transport equation represents the net effect of all internal biological, chemical, and physical transformations for each constituent. The following sections describe the source/sink formulations for each constituent modeled in CE-QUAL-W2.

The model can simulate any combination of the following constituent groups:

  • Generic constituents (conservative tracers, volatile substances)
  • Bacteria
  • Dissolved gases (N₂, total dissolved gas)
  • Water age or residence time
  • CH₄, H₂S, SO₄
  • Fe²⁺, FeOOH, Mn²⁺, MnO₂
  • Inorganic suspended solids (ISS)
  • Total dissolved solids (TDS) or salinity
  • Dissolved organic matter (labile DOM, refractory DOM)
  • Particulate organic matter (labile POM, refractory POM)
  • Organic matter variable stoichiometry (LDOM-P, RDOM-P, LPOM-P, RPOM-P, LDOM-N, RDOM-N, LPOM-N, RPOM-N)
  • Organic carbon constituents (LPOC, RPOC, LDOC, RDOC)
  • Carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD, CBODP, CBODN)
  • Algae (multiple groups with vertical migration and toxin production)
  • Periphyton/Epiphyton
  • Macrophytes
  • Zooplankton
  • Phosphorus (PO₄)
  • Ammonium (NH₄)
  • Nitrate-Nitrite (NO₃ + NO₂)
  • Dissolved silica, Particulate biogenic silica
  • Dissolved oxygen (including reaeration)
  • Organic sediments (zero-order and first-order models)
  • Sediment variable stoichiometry (P, N, C)
  • Sediment diagenesis model
  • Total inorganic carbon, alkalinity, pH, and carbonate species
  • Temperature rate multipliers

docs.title: Conservative Tracer
docs.text:
A conservative tracer has no internal sources or sinks. The source/sink term is zero:

\[ S_{tracer} = 0 \]

Conservative tracers are useful for tracking water masses from specific inflow sources such as tributaries, point sources, or nonpoint sources.

docs.title: Volatile Generic Constituent
docs.text:
For a volatile generic constituent, losses occur through gas transfer at the water surface:

\[ S_{volatile} = -K_v(\Phi - \Phi_{sat}) \]

where:

  • \(K_v\) = volatilization rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi\) = constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{sat}\) = saturation concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Bacteria
docs.text:
Bacteria are modeled with first-order decay and photodegradation. The source/sink term is:

\[ S_{bact} = -K_d \Phi_{bact} - K_{photo} \Phi_{bact} \]

where:

  • \(K_d\) = first-order decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{photo}\) = photodegradation rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{bact}\) = bacteria concentration, counts mL⁻¹ or equivalent

docs.title: Dissolved Nitrogen Gas and Total Dissolved Gas
N₂ Dissolved Gas
docs.text:
Dissolved nitrogen gas (N₂) is modeled as a generic constituent with gas transfer at the water surface. The source/sink term includes reaeration:

\[ S_{N_2} = \frac{A_{sur}}{V_{sur}} K_L(\Phi_{N_2sat} - \Phi_{N_2}) \]

where:

  • \(K_L\) = gas transfer velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{N_2sat}\) = N₂ saturation concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{N_2}\) = dissolved N₂ concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(A_{sur}\) = surface area, m²
  • \(V_{sur}\) = surface layer volume, m³

N₂ saturation is computed from temperature and atmospheric pressure using standard solubility equations.

docs.title: Total Dissolved Gas
docs.text: Total dissolved gas (TDG) pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of all dissolved gases (primarily N₂ and O₂). TDG is computed as a derived quantity from dissolved N₂ and dissolved O₂ concentrations.

docs.title: Water Age or Residence Time
docs.text:
Water age (or residence time) is a constituent that increases linearly with time:

\[ S_{age} = 1 \]

The concentration represents the elapsed time since water entered the model domain from a specific source. Water age is useful for understanding transport time scales and mixing patterns.

docs.title: Dissolved Gas Pressure
docs.text: Dissolved gas pressure is computed from the concentrations of dissolved N₂ and dissolved O₂ using Henry's Law relationships and is reported as a percentage of atmospheric pressure (percent saturation).

docs.title: Methane (CH₄)
docs.text:
Methane in the water column is produced by sediment diagenesis under anaerobic conditions and is oxidized in the presence of dissolved oxygen. The source/sink term for CH₄ is:

\[ S_{CH_4} = -K_{CH_4}\Phi_{CH_4} \]

where:

  • \(K_{CH_4}\) = CH₄ oxidation rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{CH_4}\) = CH₄ concentration, g m⁻³

CH₄ oxidation consumes dissolved oxygen according to the stoichiometric relationship.

docs.title: Hydrogen Sulfide (H₂S)
docs.text:
H₂S is produced in the sediments under anaerobic conditions through sulfate reduction and is oxidized in the water column. The source/sink term for H₂S is:

\[ S_{H_2S} = -K_{H_2S}\Phi_{H_2S} \]

where:

  • \(K_{H_2S}\) = H₂S oxidation rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{H_2S}\) = H₂S concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Sulfate (SO₄)
docs.text: SO₄ is consumed through sulfate reduction under anaerobic conditions in the sediments and water column. The source/sink term for SO₄ includes the sulfate reduction rate.

docs.title: Water Column Fe²⁺, FeOOH, Mn²⁺, MnO₂
Ferrous Iron Fe²⁺
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for Fe(II) is:

\[ S_{Fe(II)} = -\underbrace{k_{Fe(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Fe(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} + \underbrace{k_{FeOOH}\left(\frac{K_{FeOOH}}{K_{FeOOH} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{FeOOH}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

where:

  • \(k_{FeOOH}\) = reduction rate in water column, s⁻¹
  • \(k_{Fe(II)0}\) = oxidation rate in water column, s⁻¹ (g m⁻³)⁻¹
  • \(K_{FeOOH}\) = half-saturation constant for oxygen for this reaction, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{DO}\) = dissolved oxygen concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{Fe(II)}\) = ferrous iron concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{FeOOH}\) = iron oxyhydroxide concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(pH\) = pH in water column

docs.title: Iron Oxyhydroxide FeOOH
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for iron oxyhydroxide is:

\[ S_{FeOOH} = \underbrace{k_{Fe(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Fe(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} - \underbrace{k_{FeOOH}\left(\frac{K_{FeOOH}}{K_{FeOOH} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{FeOOH}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

docs.title: Mn²⁺ (Divalent Manganese)
docs.text:
The rate equation for Mn(II) in the water column is:

\[ S_{Mn(II)} = -\underbrace{k_{Mn(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Mn(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} + \underbrace{k_{MnO_2}\left(\frac{K_{MnO_2}}{K_{MnO_2} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{MnO_2}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

where:

  • \(k_{MnO_2}\) = reduction rate in water column, s⁻¹
  • \(k_{Mn(II)0}\) = oxidation rate in water column, s⁻¹ (g m⁻³)⁻¹
  • \(K_{MnO_2}\) = half-saturation constant for oxygen for this reaction, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{Mn(II)}\) = Mn(II) concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{MnO_2}\) = manganese dioxide concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Manganese Dioxide MnO₂
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for manganese dioxide is:

\[ S_{MnO_2} = \underbrace{k_{Mn(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Mn(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} - \underbrace{k_{MnO_2}\left(\frac{K_{MnO_2}}{K_{MnO_2} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{MnO_2}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

docs.title: Inorganic Suspended Solids
docs.text:
Inorganic suspended solids (ISS) are modeled as settling particles with no internal kinetic reactions other than settling:

\[ S_{ISS} = -\omega_{ISS}\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial A \Phi_{ISS}}{\partial z} \]

where:

  • \(\omega_{ISS}\) = inorganic suspended solids settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{ISS}\) = ISS concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(A\) = horizontal area, m²

Multiple ISS groups can be defined with different settling velocities and particle sizes. When ISS settles to the bottom, it is lost from the water column. Unlike organic sediments, ISS does not accumulate in the sediment compartment.

Note

In the sediment diagenesis model for Version 4.22 and earlier, there was a group for Mature Fine Tailings that was added as a generic constituent. The current model now sets this state variable as a suspended solids group.

docs.title: Total Dissolved Solids or Salinity
docs.text:
Total dissolved solids (TDS) affect water density and ionic strength, thereby affecting water movements, pH, and the distribution of carbonate species. Dissolved solids are normally expressed as TDS in freshwater applications. Estuarine applications normally use salinity.

Either TDS or salinity can be used with the choice indicated by the parameter [WTYPEC] specified in the control file. If TDS is used, the units are g m⁻³; if salinity is used, the units are kg m⁻³. TDS and salinity are not necessarily equivalent. In the model, both are treated conservatively with the rate term set to zero.

docs.title: Labile DOM
docs.text:
Because of the importance of dissolved oxygen in aquatic systems, all constituents exerting an oxygen demand must be included in kinetic formulations. This demand is often measured as the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which includes microbial respiration and metabolism of various organic and inorganic compounds. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is composed of labile and refractory components. DOM is modeled as two separate compartments because of the different decomposition rates of the two groups.

The rate equation for labile DOM is:

\[ S_{LDOM} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{LDOM}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\text{labile DOM decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality/excretion}} \tag{4-70} \]

where:

  • \(P_{am}\) = pattern coefficient for algal mortality
  • \(P_{em}\) = pattern coefficient for epiphyton mortality
  • \(P_{mm}\) = partitioning coefficient for macrophyte mortality
  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier for organic matter decay
  • \(K_{ae}\) = algal excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{am}\) = algal mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ee}\) = epiphyton excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{em}\) = epiphyton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{mm}\) = macrophyte mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = labile to refractory DOM transfer rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algal concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_e\) = epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{macro}\) = macrophyte concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Refractory DOM
docs.text:
Refractory DOM is composed of compounds in the aquatic environment that slowly decompose, exerting oxygen demand over long periods. Internally, refractory DOM is produced from the decomposition of labile DOM.

The rate equation for refractory DOM is:

\[ S_{RDOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-71} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(K_{RDOM}\) = refractory DOM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile DOM, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{RDOM}\) = refractory DOM concentration, g m⁻³

The rate terms are evaluated in subroutine REFRACTORY_DOM.

docs.title: Labile POM
docs.text:
Labile particulate organic matter (LPOM) represents particulate organic material in the water column. Decaying particulate organic matter is a source of refractory particulate organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus, and inorganic carbon. A stoichiometric relationship governs mineralization of ammonium, phosphorus, and inorganic carbon, and an oxygen demand is exerted as LPOM decomposes.

When LPOM settles to the bottom, it accumulates and decays in the sediment compartment or the sediment diagenesis compartment if activated for the simulation.

The rate equation for LPOM is:

\[ S_{LPOM} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial A\Phi_{LPOM}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}K_{mm}\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zm}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}}{\sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{LPOM}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion of LPOM}} \tag{4-72} \]

where:

  • \(P_{am}\) = partition coefficient for algal mortality
  • \(P_{em}\) = partition coefficient for epiphyton mortality
  • \(P_{mm}\) = partition coefficient for macrophyte mortality
  • \(P_{zooP}\) = partition coefficient for zooplankton LPOM grazing
  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier for organic matter
  • \(\omega_{POM}\) = POM settling rate, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{am}\) = algal mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{em}\) = epiphyton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{mm}\) = macrophyte mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{zm}\) = zooplankton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{zg}\) = zooplankton growth rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOM}\) = labile POM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{effic}\) = zooplankton ingestion efficiency
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile POM to refractory POM, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algal concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_e\) = periphyton/epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{macro}\) = macrophyte concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{LPOM}\) = detritus concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{zoo}\) = zooplankton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\sigma_{pom}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for particulate organic matter
  • \(\sigma_{alg}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for algae
  • \(\sigma_{zoo}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for zooplankton

POM settling and accumulation in the sediment compartment is handled identically to the algal compartment.

docs.title: Refractory POM
docs.text:
Refractory POM is slowly decaying non-living, organic matter that settles. The source/sink terms are first-order decay, the conversion of LPOM to RPOM, and sedimentation. The settled organic matter becomes part of the first-order sediment model or the sediment diagenesis model if they are active.

The rate equation for RPOM is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{RPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-73} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile POM to refractory POM, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{RPOM}\) = refractory POM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\omega_{POM}\) = POM settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{LPOM}\) = labile POM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{RPOM}\) = refractory POM concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Organic Matter Variable Stoichiometry
docs.text:
CE-QUAL-W2 includes variable stoichiometry of organic matter starting with Version 3.5. Previous versions used fixed stoichiometric constants for the ratios of nitrogen and phosphorus to organic matter.

Eight constituents are required to simulate the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus in labile dissolved organic matter (LDOM), refractory organic matter (RDOM), labile particulate organic matter (LPOM), and refractory particulate organic matter (RPOM). These constituents are summarized in the following table. All inputs of organic matter accumulate N and P according to the stoichiometry of the incoming organic matter.

Abbreviation Constituent LDOM-P Labile dissolved organic matter phosphorus RDOM-P Refractory dissolved organic matter phosphorus LPOM-P Labile particulate organic matter phosphorus RPOM-P Refractory particulate organic matter phosphorus LDOM-N Labile dissolved organic matter nitrogen RDOM-N Refractory dissolved organic matter nitrogen LPOM-N Labile particulate organic matter nitrogen RPOM-N Refractory particulate organic matter nitrogen

docs.title: LDOM-P
docs.text:
LDOM-P is the amount of phosphorus in labile dissolved organic matter. The rate equation for LDOM-P is:

\[ S_{\text{LDOM-P}} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LDOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\text{labile DOM-P decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM-P decay}}} \tag{4-74} \]

docs.title: RDOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for RDOM-P is:

\[ S_{RDOM-P} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-75} \]

docs.title: LPOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for LPOM-P is:

\[ S_{LPOM-P} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}P_{mpom}K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zm}\delta_{Pz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\delta_{Pz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM-P}}{\Phi_{LPOM}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOM-P}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-76} \]

docs.title: RPOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for RPOM-P is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}(1-P_{mpom})K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM-P}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-77} \]

docs.title: LDOM-N
docs.text:
LDOM-N is the amount of nitrogen in labile dissolved organic matter. The rate equation for LDOM-N is:

\[ S_{\text{LDOM-N}} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LDOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\text{labile DOM-N decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM-N decay}}} \tag{4-78} \]

docs.title: RDOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for RDOM-N is:

\[ S_{RDOM-N} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-79} \]

docs.title: LPOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for LPOM-N is:

\[ S_{LPOM-N} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}P_{mpom}K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{K_{zm}\delta_{Nz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\delta_{Nz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM-N}}{\Phi_{LPOM}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOM-N}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-80} \]

docs.title: RPOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for RPOM-N is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}(1-P_{mpom})K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM-N}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-81} \]

docs.title: Organic Carbon Constituents
docs.text:
The organic matter state variables (LPOM, RPOM, RDOM, LDOM) are based on organic matter dry weight. CE-QUAL-W2 also supports organic matter expressed as carbon (C). Many other models use this approach because organic matter is rarely measured in the field, whereas organic carbon is routinely measured. Instead of LDOM, LPOM, RDOM, and RPOM, the user can specify LDOC, LPOC, RDOC, and RPOC.

Organic matter is difficult for laboratories to measure directly. However, collective water quality parameters such as organic carbon, organic nitrogen, and organic phosphorus are commonly measured. The model includes an option for directly simulating organic carbon constituents without organic matter. The four organic carbon state variables are labile dissolved organic carbon (LDOC), refractory dissolved organic carbon (RDOC), labile particulate organic carbon (LPOC), and refractory particulate organic carbon (RPOC).

docs.title: LPOC
docs.text:
The kinetic source/sink term for LPOC is:

\[ S_{LPOC} = \underbrace{\sum K_{am}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a P_{am}}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{em}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e P_{em}}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{LPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOC}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC decay}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POC transfer}}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{LPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}P_{nom}P_{mmLPOM}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{K_{zm}\delta_{cz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum\left(Z_u\delta_{cz}\Phi_{zoo}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \Phi_{LPOM} + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo}}\right)}_{\text{zooplankton growth}} \tag{4-82} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{LPOC}\) = LPOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(P_{am}\) = fraction of algal mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(P_{em}\) = fraction of epiphyton mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(P_{mm}\) = fraction of macrophyte mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(\delta_{ca}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in algae, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{ce}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in epiphyton, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{cm}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in macrophyte, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{cz}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in zooplankton, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOC}\) = LPOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\) = transfer rate from LPOC to RPOC, s⁻¹

docs.title: RPOC
docs.text:
The kinetic source/sink term for RPOC is:

\[ S_{RPOC} = \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POC transfer}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOC}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{RPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOC}}{\partial z}}_{\text{RPOC settling}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}P_{mm}(1-P_{mmLPOM})}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} \tag{4-83} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{RPOC}\) = RPOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\) = transfer rate from LPOC to RPOC, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{RPOC}\) = RPOC decay rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: LDOC
docs.text:
The kinetic source/sink term for LDOC is:

\[ S_{LDOC} = \underbrace{\sum K_{am}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a(1-P_{am})}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{em}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e(1-P_{em})}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\text{LDOC decay}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOC transfer}}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}(1-P_{mm})}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC hydrolysis}} \tag{4-84} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{LDOC}\) = LDOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{LDOC}\) = LDOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\) = LDOC to RDOC transfer rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: RDOC
docs.text:
The kinetic source/sink term for RDOC is:

\[ S_{RDOC} = \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOC transfer}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RDOC}\Phi_{RDOC}}_{\text{RDOC decay}} \tag{4-85} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{RDOC}\) = RDOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{RDOC}\) = RDOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\) = LDOC to RDOC transfer rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: Carbonaceous Biochemical Oxygen Demand (CBOD)
docs.text:
Any number of CBOD groups with varying decay rates and either particulate or dissolved can be modeled, allowing the user to more accurately characterize various CBOD sources. Additionally, different CBOD sources can be tracked separately in the model to determine their effect on the receiving water.

When including CBOD in the simulation, ensure that CBOD, DOM, POM, and algal biomass are properly accounted for to avoid double-counting oxygen demand. CBOD is typically specified as allochthonous inputs, while autochthonous organic matter is tracked in the various organic matter compartments. This group can model dissolved or particulate CBOD by specifying a zero or a finite settling velocity, respectively. Settled CBOD enters the first-order sediment compartment.

In Version 3.6 and earlier, the CBOD cycle used fixed stoichiometry in terms of C:N:P. Starting with Version 3.7, the nitrogen and phosphorus corresponding to each CBOD group are modeled as separate constituents.

The rate equation for CBOD is:

\[ S_{CBOD} = -\underbrace{\Theta^{T-20}K_{BOD}R_{BOD}\Phi_{CBOD}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{CBOD}\frac{\partial R_{BOD}\Phi_{CBOD}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-86} \]

where:

  • \(\Theta\) = BOD temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(\omega_{CBOD}\) = CBOD settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{BOD}\) = CBOD decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(R_{BOD}\) = CBOD conversion from input CBOD to CBOD-ultimate (CBODᵤ)
  • \(\Phi_{CBOD}\) = CBOD concentration, g m⁻³

Note

The model accepts 5-day CBOD₅ or any other day CBOD as input. The \(R_{BOD}\) term converts to CBODᵤ (ultimate or 28-day) internally. The model outputs CBOD in the same form as the input (e.g., CBOD₅ if CBOD₅ was entered). If CBODᵤ is used as input, set \(R_{BOD}\) = 1.

Typical determination of \(R_{BOD}\) is based on the following standard CBOD equation:

\[ R_{BOD} = \frac{CBOD_u}{CBOD_t} = \frac{1}{1 - \exp(-K_{BOD} t)} \]

where \(t\) is the time in days (5 days, for example), \(K_{BOD}\) is the BOD decay rate in day⁻¹, and \(CBOD_t\) is the CBOD at that time.

docs.title: CBODP
docs.text:
The phosphorus associated with a specific CBOD group is modeled as a separate constituent. The rate equation for CBODP is:

\[ S_{CBODP} = -\underbrace{\Theta^{T-20}K_{BOD}\Phi_{CBODP}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{CBOD}\frac{\partial \Phi_{CBODP}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \]

where:

  • \(\Theta\) = BOD temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(\omega_{CBOD}\) = CBOD settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{BOD}\) = CBOD decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{CBODP}\) = CBODP concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: CBODN
docs.text:
