\[ \Delta t \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \int_\eta^h q \, BU_x \, dz \approx \Delta t \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \sum_{kt}^{kb} qU_x BH_r \tag{5-26} \] \[ \int_\eta^h qB \, dz \approx \sum_{kt}^{kb} qBH_r \tag{5-27} \]

docs.title: Tridiagonal System for η
docs.text:
Combining these terms into one equation:

\[ A \eta_{i-1}^n + X \eta_i^n + C \eta_{i+1}^n = D \tag{5-28} \]

where:

\[ A = \left[ \frac{-g\cos\alpha \, \Delta t^2}{\Delta x} \sum_{kt}^{kb} BH_r \bigg|_{i-1} \right] \] \[ X = \left[ B_\eta \Delta x + \frac{g\cos\alpha \, \Delta t^2}{\Delta x} \left\{ \sum_{kt}^{kb} BH_r \bigg|_i + \sum_{kt}^{kb} BH_r \bigg|_{i-1} \right\} \right] \] \[ C = \left[ \frac{-g\cos\alpha \, \Delta t^2}{\Delta x} \sum_{kt}^{kb} BH_r \bigg|_i \right] \] \[ D = \Delta t \sum_{kt}^{kb} (UBH_r|_i - UBH_r|_{i-1}) + B_\eta \eta_i^{n-1} \Delta x + \Delta t^2 \sum_{kt}^{kb} (FH_r|_i - FH_r|_{i-1}) \] \[ + \Delta t^2 g \sin\alpha \sum_{kt}^{kb} (BH_r|_i - BH_r|_{i-1}) + \Delta t^2 \frac{g\cos\alpha}{\rho} \sum_{kt}^{kb} (BH_r|_i - BH_r|_{i-1}) \sum_{kt}^{kb} \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} H_r \] \[ + \Delta x \Delta t \sum_{kt}^{kb} qBH_r + \Delta x \Delta t^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \sum_{kt}^{kb} qU_x BH_r + \frac{\Delta t^2}{\rho} \left[ \left( B\tau_{xz}|_h - B\tau_{xz}|_\eta \right)_i - \left( B\tau_{xz}|_h - B\tau_{xz}|_\eta \right)_{i-1} \right] \]

This equation is applied at all cells in the branch, generating a system of equations that are solved for the water surface elevation at the \(n+1\) time level using the Thomas algorithm. The resulting FDA is implicit in η because of the dependence of η in the momentum equation.

The boundary conditions of either flow or head boundary are accounted for in applying the above equation to the boundary cells as shown in Figure 125 and Figure 126, respectively. The boundary condition implementation is the same as described in Cole and Buchak (1995).

docs.title: Horizontal Momentum Numerical Solution for Horizontal Velocity U
docs.text:
The x-momentum equation:

\[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z} = gB\sin\alpha + g\cos\alpha B \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho} \int_\eta^z \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} \, dz + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xz}}{\partial z} + qBU_x \tag{5-29} \]

is solved using either a fully explicit or an explicit/implicit finite difference solution technique specified by the user after the water surface equation is solved.

docs.title: Explicit Solution
docs.text:
This scheme solves the partial differential terms using an explicit finite difference technique where:

\[ U_i^{n+1} B_i^{n+1} = U_i^n B_i^n + \Delta t \left\{ -\frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z} + gB\sin\alpha + g\cos\alpha B \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho} \int_\eta^z \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} \, dz + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xz}}{\partial z} + qBU_x \right\}_i^n \tag{5-30} \]

The various terms are put into finite difference form as follows. The longitudinal advection of momentum is an upwind difference scheme where the order of differencing depends on the sign of \(U\), e.g., for \(U > 0\):

\[ \frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x}\bigg|_{i,k} \cong \frac{1}{\Delta x_i} \left[ B_{i,k}^n U_{i,k}^n U_{i,k}^n - B_{i-1,k}^n U_{i-1,k}^n U_{i-1,k}^n \right] \tag{5-31} \]

The vertical advection of momentum is also an upwind scheme based on the velocity of \(W\). For \(W > 0\) or downward flow:

\[ \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z}\bigg|_{i,k} \cong \frac{1}{\Delta z_k} \left[ \left( W_{i,k}^n U_{i,k}^n B_{i,k}^n \right) - \left( W_{i,k-1}^n U_{i,k-1}^n B_{i,k-1}^n \right) \right] \tag{5-32} \]

The gravity force is:

\[ gB\sin\alpha = g\sin\alpha \, B_i^n \tag{5-33} \]

The pressure gradient is:

\[ g\cos\alpha \, B \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho} \int_\eta^z \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} \, dz = \frac{g\cos\alpha B_i^n}{\Delta x} (\eta_{i+1} - \eta_i)^n - \frac{g\cos\alpha B_i^n}{\rho \Delta x} \sum \left( \rho_{i+1,k} - \rho_{i,k} \right)^n \Delta z_k \tag{5-34} \]

The horizontal advection of turbulent momentum is:

\[ \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial BA_x \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}}{\partial x} = \left( \frac{B_{i+1/2}^n A_x}{\Delta x_i \Delta x_{i+1/2}} \right) \left( U_{i+1,k}^n - U_{i,k}^n \right) - \left( \frac{B_{i-1/2}^n A_x}{\Delta x_i \Delta x_{i-1/2}} \right) \left( U_{i,k}^n - U_{i-1,k}^n \right) \tag{5-35} \]

The contribution to longitudinal momentum by lateral branch inflows is:

\[ qBU_x = qBU_x \big|_{i,k}^n \tag{5-36} \]

Using the definition of the shear stress:

\[ \tau_{xz} = \left[ \tau_w + \tau_b + \rho A_z \frac{\partial U}{\partial z} \right] \tag{5-37} \]

where \(A_z\) is the turbulent kinematic viscosity, the vertical transport of momentum is:

\[ \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xz}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \frac{B}{\rho} \left[ \tau_w + \tau_b + \rho A_z \frac{\partial U}{\partial z} \right] = \left( \frac{B_{i,k+1/2}^n}{\Delta z_k \Delta z_{k+1/2} \rho} \right) \left[ \tau_w|_{i,k+1/2}^n + \tau_b|_{i,k+1/2}^n + \frac{\rho A_z \bigg|_{i,k+1/2}}{\Delta z_{k+1/2}} \left( U_{i,k+1}^n - U_{i,k}^n \right) \right] - \left( \frac{B_{i,k-1/2}^n}{\Delta z_k \Delta z_{k-1/2} \rho} \right) \left[ \tau_w|_{i,k-1/2}^n + \tau_b|_{i,k-1/2}^n + \frac{\rho A_z \bigg|_{i,k-1/2}}{\Delta z_{k-1/2}} \left( U_{i,k}^n - U_{i,k-1}^n \right) \right] \tag{5-38} \]

docs.title: Implicit Solution
docs.text:
The implicit technique was utilized to reduce the time step limitation for numerical stability when values of \(A_z\) were large, as for an estuary or a river system. This occurs because the time step limitation is a function of \(A_z\). Only the vertical transport of momentum term was solved implicitly. All other terms for the solution of the horizontal momentum equation were the same as the explicit scheme.

The horizontal momentum equation can be separated into the following two equations:

\[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z} = gB\sin\alpha + g\cos\alpha B \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho} \int_\eta^z \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} \, dz + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B(\tau_b + \tau_w)}{\partial z} + qBU_x \tag{5-39} \] \[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( BA_z \frac{\partial U}{\partial z} \right) \tag{5-40} \]

Equation 5-39 is written as:

\[ U_i^* B_i^{n+1} = U_i^n B_i^n + \Delta t \left\{ -\frac{\partial UUB}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial WUB}{\partial z} + gB\sin\alpha + g\cos\alpha B \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} - \frac{g\cos\alpha B}{\rho} \int_\eta^z \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} \, dz + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial B(\tau_b + \tau_w)}{\partial z} + qBU_x \right\}_i^n \tag{5-41} \]

where \(U^*\) is the velocity at the new time level before the application of Equation 5-40. Equation 5-39 is solved similarly to the solution of the fully explicit technique outlined above.

Equation 5-40 is then solved using a fully implicit technique as:

\[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial t} = \frac{(U_i^{n+1}B_i^{n+1} - U_i^*B_i^{n+1})}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( \rho B^{n+1} A_z \frac{\partial U^{n+1}}{\partial z} \right) \tag{5-42} \]

This can be rewritten as:

\[ U_i^{n+1} B_i^{n+1} = U_i^* B_i^{n+1} + \left( \frac{\Delta t B_{i,k+1/2}^{n+1}}{\Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k+1/2}}{\Delta z_{k+1/2}} \left( U_{i,k+1}^{n+1} - U_{i,k}^{n+1} \right) \right] - \left( \frac{\Delta t B_{i,k-1/2}^{n+1}}{\Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k-1/2}}{\Delta z_{k-1/2}} \left( U_{i,k}^{n+1} - U_{i,k-1}^{n+1} \right) \right] \tag{5-43} \]

Regrouping terms at \(n+1\) time level on the LHS, the equation can be written as:

\[ A U_{i,k-1}^{n+1} + V U_{i,k}^{n+1} + C U_{i,k+1}^{n+1} = D U_{i,k}^* \tag{5-44} \]

where:

\[ A = \left( \frac{-\Delta t B_{i,k-1/2}^{n+1}}{B_{i,k}^{n+1} \Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k-1/2}}{\Delta z_{k-1/2}} \right] \] \[ V = 1 + \left( \frac{\Delta t B_{i,k+1/2}^{n+1}}{B_{i,k}^{n+1} \Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k+1/2}}{\Delta z_{k+1/2}} \right] + \left( \frac{\Delta t B_{i,k-1/2}^{n+1}}{B_{i,k}^{n+1} \Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k-1/2}}{\Delta z_{k-1/2}} \right] \] \[ C = \left( \frac{-\Delta t B_{i,k+1/2}^{n+1}}{B_{i,k}^{n+1} \Delta z_k} \right) \left[ \frac{A_z \bigg|_{i,k+1/2}}{\Delta z_{k+1/2}} \right] \] \[ D = 1 \]

The resulting simultaneous equations are solved for \(U^{n+1}\) using the Thomas algorithm.

The resulting horizontal velocities are then corrected to preserve branch continuity (or more correctly to "force" continuity). The lack of a continuity balance is a result of numerical errors in the solution of the FDAs for \(\eta^n\) and \(U^{n+1}\). Cole and Buchak (1995) discuss the algorithm to correct horizontal velocities from continuity.

The correction is calculated segment by segment: the change in the water layers over time should equal the net flow into the segment by horizontal velocities. The change or correction in velocity is apportioned equally to the horizontal velocity of all vertical layers. Other numerical models iterate by re-solving the water surface equation after updated horizontal and vertical velocities are computed, which results in significant computational time but a more correct solution.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: The solution of the horizontal momentum equation can either accept a flow boundary condition (as shown in Figure 127) or a head or water level condition (as shown in Figure 128). For the flow boundary condition, the velocities at the flow boundary are specified based on the flow rates provided by the user. For the head condition, the model user sets the head or water level as a function of time.

docs.title: Solution of Vertical Velocity W
docs.text:
The continuity equation

\[ \frac{\partial UB}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WB}{\partial z} = qB \]

is used to solve for \(W\) after discretizing into finite differences as:

\[ \frac{WB_{i,k} - WB_{i,k-1}}{\Delta z_k} = -\left( \frac{UB_{i,k} - UB_{i-1,k}}{\Delta x_i} \right) + q_{i,k} B_{i,k} \tag{5-45} \]

The algorithm starts at the bottom cell using corrected horizontal velocities and where \(WB_{k=0} = 0\) such that:

\[ WB_{i,k-1} = -WB_{i,k} + \Delta z_k \left( \frac{UB_{i,k} - UB_{i-1,k}}{\Delta x_i} \right) - \Delta z_k q_{i,k} B_{i,k} \]

docs.title: Numerical Stability
docs.text:
The numerical stability criterion is based on the following equation that only considers momentum equation stability:

\[ \Delta t \leq \frac{1}{2\left(\frac{A_x}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{A_z}{\Delta z^2}\right) + \frac{Q}{V} + \frac{\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho} gH}}{2\Delta x}} \tag{5-46} \]

where:

Symbol Description Units \(\Delta t\) time step s \(A_x\) longitudinal eddy viscosity m² s⁻¹ \(A_z\) vertical eddy viscosity m² s⁻¹ \(Q\) total flow into or out of a cell m³ s⁻¹ \(V\) cell volume m³ \(g\) gravitational acceleration m s⁻² \(H\) maximum waterbody depth m \(\rho\) water density kg m⁻³ \(\Delta\rho\) surface to bottom water density difference kg m⁻³

Warning

This criterion does NOT guarantee numerical stability since it is based on a linearized form of the PDEs. There is no check on stability for the advective-diffusion equation since it is usually not limiting. However, the advective-diffusion equation can also become unstable.

docs.title: Characteristics of the Constituent Numerical Solution
docs.text:
• The advective-diffusion equation is solved by splitting the solution between horizontal and vertical transport.
  • The horizontal transport is solved explicitly where QUICKEST (Quadratic Upstream Interpolation for Convective Kinematics with Estimated Streaming Terms, a third-order numerical scheme, Leonard, 1979) is used for horizontal explicit transport, and central differences are used for diffusion.
  • Vertical transport is solved using an implicit/explicit general time-weighted scheme for advection and a fully implicit scheme for diffusion; simultaneous equations are solved using the Thomas algorithm.

docs.title: Solution of the Advective-Diffusion Equation
docs.text:
The advective-diffusion transport equation

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UB\Phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial \left(BD_x \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x}\right)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial \left(BD_z \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z}\right)}{\partial z} = q_\Phi B + S_\Phi B \]

is solved by splitting the two-dimensional FDA into two one-dimensional parts: (1) horizontal transport and sources/sinks and lateral inflows/outflows, and (2) vertical transport.

docs.title: Horizontal Transport
docs.text:
The horizontal part of the solution is:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} \cong \frac{B\Phi_{i,k}^* - B\Phi_{i,k}^n}{\Delta t} \cong \left[ -\frac{\partial UB\Phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \left(BD_x \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x}\right)}{\partial x} + q_\Phi B + S_\Phi B \right]_{i,k}^n \tag{5-47} \]

The time level \(*\) is the intermediate concentration (or temperature) considering only horizontal fluxes, sources/sinks, and lateral inflows. In this step, the diffusion term is a central spatial difference and the advection term uses the ULTIMATE/QUICKEST differencing technique (see discussion below).

In Version 2, the QUICKEST scheme was introduced, which uses quadratic upstream differencing rather than linear upstream differencing. Cole and Buchak (1995) discuss this differencing algorithm, which eliminates much of the numerical diffusion associated with upstream differencing.

docs.title: Vertical Transport
docs.text:
The result from this explicit computation is then used to compute the vertical transport (see Figure 131). The resulting FDA is put in a general time-weighted scheme:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} \cong \frac{B\Phi_{i,k}^{n+1} - B\Phi_{i,k}^*}{\Delta t} \cong \left(-\theta \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z}\right)_{i,k}^n + \left(-(1-\theta) \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z}\right)_{i,k}^{n+1} + \left(\frac{\partial \left(BD_z \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z}\right)}{\partial z}\right)_{i,k}^{n+1} \tag{5-48} \]

where θ is the degree of implicitness (=0 explicit; =0.5 Crank-Nicholson; =1 fully implicit). Central differences are used for the spatial derivatives for both the vertical diffusion and vertical advection terms. This equation is applied to all vertical layers and solved using the Thomas algorithm. The model user can choose the degree of implicitness for this equation.

docs.title: Advective Transport in x and z
docs.text:
The first step in the numerical solution is to define the computational grid (Figure 132). The grid is space-staggered since some state variables are defined at the segment centers and some at segment interfaces, displaced by \(\Delta x/2\) or \(\Delta z/2\) from the segment center. The grid discretizes a waterbody into computational cells whose locations are defined by their segment I and layer number K, i.e., cell (K,I).

Variables defined at the cell boundary include the horizontal and vertical velocities (\(U\) and \(W\)), longitudinal eddy viscosity and diffusivity (\(A_x\) and \(D_x\)), vertical eddy viscosity and diffusivity (\(A_z\) and \(D_z\)), and internal shear stress \(\tau_x\). Variables defined at the cell center include the density (\(\rho\)), temperature (\(T\)), constituent concentration (Φ), pressure (\(P\)), and average cell width (\(B\)).

Since constituent concentration is defined at the center and velocities are defined at the boundaries, spatial averaging of velocities is not required to determine fluxes into or out of the control volume at a fixed time level. The horizontal velocity is surrounded by a cell with water surface elevations and densities defined on either side, so it is computed from horizontal gradients of the surface slope and densities without requiring spatial averaging of these variables.

The geometry is specified by a cell width, \(B\), thickness or vertical grid spacing, \(H\) or \(\Delta z\), and length, \(\Delta x\). Several additional geometric variables are used in the calculations. These additional variables include the average cross-sectional area between two cells (k,i) and (k,i+1):

\[ BH_{r_{k,i}} = \frac{B_{k,i} H_{k,i} + B_{k,i} H_{k,i+1}}{2} \tag{5-49} \]

the average widths between two cells (k,i) and (k+1,i):

\[ B_{b_{k,i}} = \frac{B_{k,i} + B_{k+1,i}}{2} \tag{5-50} \]

and the average layer thickness between layers k and k+1:

\[ \overline{H}_{k,i} = \frac{H_k + H_{k+1}}{2} \tag{5-51} \]

The numerical procedure for solving the six unknowns at each timestep is to first compute water surface elevations. With the new surface elevations, new horizontal velocities can be computed, and with new horizontal velocities, the vertical velocities can be found from continuity.

Using new horizontal and vertical velocities, the water surface elevation equation can be solved for η simultaneously for a model branch. The solution for η is thus spatially implicit at the same time level and eliminates the surface gravity wave speed criterion:

\[ \Delta t < \frac{\Delta x}{\sqrt{g H_{max}}} \tag{5-52} \]

that can seriously limit timesteps in deep waterbodies. Then the temperature and constituent concentrations are computed from the energy and constituent mass balance equations.

docs.title: Numerical Diffusion with Upwind Differencing
docs.text:
Version 1.0 used upwind differencing in the constituent transport advective terms, in which the cell concentration immediately upstream of the velocity was used to calculate mass fluxes. A major problem with upwind differencing is the introduction of numerical diffusion, which acts like physical diffusion but is an artifact of the numerical scheme. The false longitudinal diffusion coefficient (m² s⁻¹) added to the model can be computed from:

\[ \alpha_e = \frac{u \Delta x}{2}(1 - C) \tag{5-53} \]

where:

Symbol Description \(\alpha_e\) numerical diffusion coefficient, m² s⁻¹ \(u\) velocity, m s⁻¹ \(\Delta x\) longitudinal grid spacing, m \(C\) Courant number = \(\frac{u \Delta t}{\Delta x}\)

A similar condition holds for vertical advection. In many cases, numerical diffusion can overwhelm physical diffusion, producing inaccurate results when strong gradients are present. The problem is particularly pronounced for stratified reservoirs and estuaries.

Numerical diffusion has been reduced by implementing an explicit, third-order accurate QUICKEST horizontal/vertical transport scheme (Leonard, 1979), and time-weighted, implicit vertical advection. Tests of this scheme are reported in Chapman and Cole (1992).

docs.title: Non-Uniform Grid QUICKEST Formulation
docs.text:
QUICKEST uses an additional spatial term to estimate concentrations used in computing horizontal and vertical fluxes. A nonuniform grid QUICKEST scheme was developed using a three-point Lagrangian interpolation function to estimate constituent values at grid cell interfaces. Specifically, advective multipliers for each of three upstream weighted grid cells are derived in terms of cell lengths and the local cell interface velocity. Time-invariant parts of the interpolation functions are calculated once, thus minimizing computations for additional constituents.

Implicit vertical transport including variable layer heights has also been implemented. Vertical diffusion is fully implicit, and advection employs a time-weighted, central difference, implicit scheme. A unique feature of vertical advection in the explicit part of the time-weighted scheme is QUICKEST, which increases overall accuracy.

As implemented in the code, the transport scheme is a two-part solution for constituent concentrations at the new timestep:

  1. Horizontal advection is computed using QUICKEST and diffusion is computed using central differencing. This part also includes the explicit vertical advection contribution (which utilizes QUICKEST) and all sources and sinks.
  2. The implicit part of vertical advection and diffusion are included. Diffusion is always fully implicit.

The user can time-weight advection by specifying a value for [THETA] that varies from 0 to 1:

  • For THETA equal to 0, the solution is explicit in time and vertical advection is accounted for in the first part of the algorithm.
  • For THETA equal to 1, the solution is fully implicit in time and vertical advection is accounted for in the second part of the algorithm.
  • For THETA equal to 0.5 or greater, a Crank-Nicholson scheme results where vertical advection is time-weighted between the explicit (using QUICKEST) and implicit parts.

The following is a description of QUICKEST, the preferred transport scheme.

docs.title: QUICKEST Derivation
docs.text:
In one dimension, the conservative control volume advective transport of a constituent Φ integrated over a timestep is:

\[ \Phi_i^{n+1} = \Phi_i^n - \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}(U_r \Phi_r^n - U_l \Phi_l^n) \tag{5-54} \]

where:

Symbol Description Units \(\Phi_i\) constituent concentration at a grid point g m⁻³ \(\Phi_{r,l}\) right and left cell face constituent concentrations g m⁻³ \(U_{r,l}\) right and left cell face velocity m s⁻¹ \(t\) time s

The QUICKEST algorithm was originally derived using an upstream weighted quadratic interpolation function defined over three uniformly spaced grid points. This interpolation function estimates cell face concentrations required by the conservative control volume transport scheme. For example, the right cell face concentration estimate for a flow positive to the right is:

\[ \Phi_r = T_{i-1} \Phi_{i-1} + T_i \Phi_i + T_{i+1} \Phi_{i+1} \tag{5-55} \]

where \(T\) are advective multipliers which weight the contribution of three adjacent grid point concentrations.

The advective multipliers are obtained by collecting terms associated with each constituent defined by the QUICKEST advection operator. For a non-uniform grid, a combination of two and three-point Lagrangian interpolation functions (Henrici, 1964) are used to compute the QUICKEST estimate for the right cell face concentration centered about cells i and i+1:

\[ \Phi_r = P_1(x) - \frac{U \Delta t}{2} P_2(x) + \left[ D_x \Delta t - \frac{1}{6}\left[\Delta x^2 - (U \Delta t)^2\right] \right] P_2''(x) \tag{5-56} \]

where:

  • \(x\) = the local right cell face position
  • \(D_x\) = diffusion coefficient

Defining a local coordinate system of three non-uniformly spaced grid cells denoted by \(x_{i-1}\), \(x_i\), and \(x_{i+1}\) with corresponding constituent values, the interpolation functions required in Equation 5-56 are:

\[ P_1(x) = \frac{(x - x_i)}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)} \Phi_{i+1} + \frac{(x_{i+1} - x)}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)} \Phi_i \tag{5-57} \] \[ P_2(x) = \frac{(x - x_i)(x - x_{i-1})}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)(x_{i+1} - x_{i-1})} \Phi_{i+1} + \frac{(x - x_{i+1})(x - x_{i-1})}{(x_i - x_{i+1})(x_i - x_{i-1})} \Phi_i + \frac{(x_{i+1})(x - x_i)}{(x_{i-1} - x_{i+1})(x_{i-1} - x_i)} \Phi_{i-1} \tag{5-58} \]

Taking the first derivative of \(P_1(x)\) and the second derivative of \(P_2(x)\) and substituting into Equation 5-56, it is then possible to group terms and obtain the advective multipliers. For example, the \(T_{i+1}\) multiplier is:

\[ T_{i+1} = \frac{(x - x_i)}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)} - \frac{U \Delta t}{2} \frac{[(x - x_i) + (x - x_{i-1})]}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)(x_{i+1} - x_{i-1})} + \frac{2\left(D_x \Delta t - \frac{1}{6}[\Delta x_i^2 - (U \Delta t)^2]\right)}{(x_{i+1} - x_i)(x_{i+1} - x_{i-1})} \tag{5-59} \]

Similar functions are obtained for \(T_i\) and \(T_{i-1}\) multipliers that complete the formulation for the QUICKEST algorithm.

From a computational standpoint, most geometric components of the multipliers are time-invariant and are computed once and stored in arrays. The time-varying part of the multipliers (\(U\), \(\Delta t\), \(D_x\)) are updated each timestep during computation of the \(T\) arrays. However, when the QUICKEST scheme is applied vertically, the spatial part of the multipliers for layers KT and KT+1 are updated each timestep to accommodate the surface elevation fluctuation.

docs.title: ULTIMATE/QUICKEST Numerical Transport Solution Scheme
docs.text:
In Version 2, the QUICKEST numerical scheme replaced the upwind numerical scheme used in Version 1 for solving the advective terms in the advection-diffusion equation. Compared to the upwind scheme, QUICKEST resulted in improved numerical accuracy in simulating sharp fronts since the upwind transport scheme adds excessive numerical diffusion.

A problem with the QUICKEST scheme is that it can give rise to spurious oscillations at the leading and trailing edge of a sharp front or gradient. This can occur where there are fresh/salt water interfaces, point source discharges, or cases of strong temperature stratification. Even though the upwind scheme always gives physically realistic solutions, it introduces numerical diffusion that artificially reduces sharp gradients.

An improvement was introduced by Leonard (1991) that eliminated spurious oscillations but preserved the higher-order solution scheme of QUICKEST. This technique is a Universal Limiter for Transient Interpolation Modeling of the Advective Transport Equations (ULTIMATE), a limiter for maintaining monotonic profiles near a gradient that can be applied to numerical schemes other than QUICKEST.

docs.title: Formulation for Uniform Velocity and Grid Spacing
docs.text:
In order to illustrate the scheme, consider the solution of the unsteady advective equation:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial BU\Phi}{\partial x} = 0 \tag{5-60} \]

where:

Symbol Description Units Φ concentration g m⁻³ \(B\) width m \(U\) velocity m s⁻¹ \(x\) longitudinal coordinate m \(t\) time s

The finite difference scheme for this based on a positive flow (\(U > 0\)) is:

\[ \Phi_i^{n+1} = \frac{1}{B_i^{n+1}} \left( B_i^n \Phi_i^n - \left\{ \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R \Phi_R - \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_L \Phi_L \right\} \right) \tag{5-61} \]

The value \(i\) refers to the center grid point, \(R\) is the right-hand face value, and \(L\) is the left-hand face value.

For positive flow (Figure 133):

Symbol Description Units \(\Phi_{i-1}\) upstream concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_i\) center concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_{i+1}\) downstream concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_L\) left face concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_R\) right face concentration g m⁻³ \(U_r\) right face horizontal velocity m s⁻¹

For negative flow (Figure 134):

Symbol Description Units \(\Phi_{i-1}\) downstream concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_i\) center concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_{i+1}\) upstream concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_L\) left face concentration g m⁻³ \(\Phi_R\) right face concentration g m⁻³ \(U_L\) left face horizontal velocity m s⁻¹

The term \(U \Delta t / \Delta x\) is called the Courant number. The problem to resolve is how to choose the concentrations at the "face" values since concentrations are defined at the center of a cell. An upwinding scheme sets the concentration at the left face to \(\Phi_{i-1}\) and the concentration at the right face to \(\Phi_i\) for positive flow. Higher-order numerical techniques, such as QUICKEST (Leonard, 1979), improve numerical accuracy in estimating these face values.

In CE-QUAL-W2, \(\Phi_R\) and \(\Phi_L\) are initially computed based on the QUICKEST method. However, if the criteria for a monotonic solution are violated, the values for \(\Phi_R\) and \(\Phi_L\) are revised to ensure a monotonic solution. This is the essence of the ULTIMATE algorithm that eliminates over/undershoots in the numerical transport scheme.

docs.title: Monotonicity Criteria
docs.text:
To outline the procedure for simple conditions, the velocity, segment spacing, and segment widths are assumed constant, so that Equation 5-61 can be written as:

\[ \Phi_i^{n+1} = \left( \Phi_i^n - \left\{ \left[\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right] \Phi_R - \left[\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right] \Phi_L \right\} \right) \tag{5-62} \]

Defining normalized variables based on:

\[ \widetilde{\Phi} = \frac{\Phi - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n} \tag{5-63} \]

for location \(i\) (the center location) and the right face value for positive flow, we have the following:

\[ \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n = \frac{\Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n} \tag{5-64} \] \[ \widetilde{\Phi}_R = \frac{\Phi_R - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n} \tag{5-65} \]

The conditions for a monotonic solution are:

If \(\widetilde{\Phi}_R \leq \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}_i^n}{\left[\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R}\) for \(0 < \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n \leq 1\):

\[ \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n \leq \widetilde{\Phi}_R \leq 1 \quad \text{for } 0 < \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n \leq 1 \tag{5-66} \] \[ \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n = \widetilde{\Phi}_R \quad \text{for } \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n < 0 \text{ or } \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n > 1 \tag{5-67} \]

The face value is unadjusted from that computed by the numerical scheme and the QUICKEST value of \(\Phi_R\) is used without alteration. These conditions are shown as the shaded region in Figure 135.

If these conditions are not met, then \(\Phi_R\) is adjusted to force a monotonic solution. The value of the face is replaced with the nearest allowable value of \(\widetilde{\Phi}_R\) based on the above criteria that will ensure these criteria are met. The face value is determined by using:

\[ \Phi_R = \Phi_{i-1}^n + \widetilde{\Phi}_R (\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n) \tag{5-68} \]

This procedure is applied to all the faces and then Equation 5-61 is solved to update the concentration at the next time level. This means that the right face concentration will be the left face concentration for the next segment, thus ensuring mass conservation.

According to tests performed by Lin and Falconer (1997), the QUICKEST-ULTIMATE scheme with splitting of the diffusion and source/sink terms conserved mass and eliminated numerical oscillations. Leonard (1991) also indicated that the QUICKEST scheme coupled with the ULTIMATE scheme was numerically accurate and cost-effective in terms of computational time.

Note

For any case of unequal grid spacing, the order of accuracy diminishes. Leonard (1991) recommends that if used with non-uniform grid spacing, the formal accuracy of the method is only preserved if the grid does not expand or contract more than about 125%.

Tip

Even though the ULTIMATE scheme can be used with any suitable numerical technique, Leonard (1991) indicates that when coupled with the 3rd-order QUICKEST scheme and a 2nd-order central difference diffusion operator, the results are virtually indistinguishable from other higher-order advection solvers.

docs.title: Procedure for Variable Velocities and Grid Spacing
docs.text:
The following shows a straightforward procedure by Leonard to compute the right and left face values if they do not meet the monotonic criteria, as well as a procedure for variable velocities.

Based on the sign of the velocity for each face, compute DEL:

\[ \text{DEL} = \Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n \tag{5-69} \]

If \(|\text{DEL}| < 10^{-5}\), set \(\Phi_{face} = \Phi_i^n\) and proceed to the next face (the face value is the L or R face). Otherwise, compute:

\[ \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n = \frac{\Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n} = \frac{\Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\text{DEL}} \tag{5-70} \]

If \(\widetilde{\Phi}_i^n < 0\) or \(\widetilde{\Phi}_i^n > 1\), set \(\Phi_{face} = \Phi_i^n\) and proceed to the next face. If not, compute:

\[ \widetilde{\Phi}_{face} = \frac{\Phi_{face} - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n} = \frac{\Phi_{face} - \Phi_{i-1}^n}{\text{DEL}} \tag{5-71} \]

where \(\Phi_{face}\) is computed based on the user's chosen numerical scheme (such as QUICKEST or another scheme).

  1. If \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} < \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n\), \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} = \widetilde{\Phi}_i^n\)
  2. If \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} > \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}_i^n}{\left(\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right)}\), \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} = \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}_i^n}{\left(\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right)}\)
  3. If \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} > 1\), \(\widetilde{\Phi}_{face} = 1\)

Then recompute the face value according to \(\Phi_{face} = \widetilde{\Phi}_{face} \cdot \text{DEL} + \Phi_i^n\).

Once all the face values are determined, use the finite difference form of the solution (Equation 5-61) to determine the solution.

docs.title: Optimized ULTIMATE/QUICKEST Procedure
docs.text:
Leonard (1991) also showed a numerical technique that minimized the computational burden when using ULTIMATE with the QUICKEST scheme. This technique is described as follows.

Based on the sign of the velocity for each face, define C, D, and U nodes (center, downstream, and upstream) corresponding for positive flow to \(i\), \(i+1\), and \(i-1\), respectively.

Compute DEL and CURV, where \(\text{DEL} = \Phi_{i+1}^n - \Phi_i^n\) and \(\text{CURV} = \Phi_{i+1}^n - 2\Phi_i^n + \Phi_{i-1}^n\).

  1. If \(|\text{CURV}| \leq 0.6|\text{DEL}|\), then use the QUICKEST computed value for the face value, \(\Phi_{face}\) (the face value is the R or L face as shown in Figure 137).
  2. If not, and if \(|\text{CURV}| \geq |\text{DEL}|\), then set \(\Phi_{face} = \Phi_i^n\)
  3. If not, and \(\text{DEL} > 0\), limit \(\Phi_{face}\) by \(\Phi_i^n\) below, or the smaller of \(\Phi_{reference} = \Phi_{i-1}^n + \frac{(\Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n)}{\left(\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right)}\) and \(\Phi_{i+1}^n\)
  4. If not, and \(\text{DEL} < 0\), limit \(\Phi_{face}\) by \(\Phi_i^n\), or the larger of \(\Phi_{reference} = \Phi_{i-1}^n + \frac{(\Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n)}{\left(\frac{U\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right)}\) and \(\Phi_{i+1}^n\)
  5. Once all the face values are determined, use Equation 5-61 to obtain the solution.

docs.title: Conditions for Variable Velocity and Width
docs.text:
The procedure outlined above is based on unidirectional and uniform magnitude velocity and segment widths. If the velocity regime and widths are variable, then the following procedure is followed in order to maintain a monotonic solution.

Assuming that \(U_R\) is positive and the concentration times width (\(\Phi B\)) increases monotonically, i.e., \((B\Phi)_{i-1}^n < (B\Phi)_i^n < (B\Phi)_{i+1}^n < (B\Phi)_{i+2}^n\), between segment \(i-1\) and \(i+2\), then the goal of the technique is to estimate \(\Phi_R\), or really \(B_R \Phi_R\), and to update the concentration using Equation 5-61. Equation 5-61 can be written as a condition for \(\Phi_R\) as:

\[ \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R \Phi_R = B_i^n \Phi_i^n - \Phi_i^{n+1} B_i^{n+1} + \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_L \Phi_L \tag{5-72} \]

If it is assumed that \(B_i^n \Phi_i^n \leq B_R \Phi_R \leq B_{i+1} \Phi_{i+1}^n\), then this is equivalent to saying that \(B_i^n U_i^n \Phi_i^n \leq B_R^n U_R^n \Phi_R \leq B_{i+1}^n U_{i+1}^n \Phi_{i+1}^n\), or that the net flux into a segment is increasing.

Using the monotonic limitation that \(B_i^{n+1} \Phi_i^{n+1} \geq B_{i-1} \Phi_{i-1}^n\) then Equation 5-72 becomes:

\[ \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R \Phi_R \leq B_i^n \Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n B_{i-1}^n + \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_L \Phi_L \tag{5-73} \]

Then making a conservative assumption that \(B_L \Phi_L \geq B_{i-1} \Phi_{i-1}^n\), Equation 5-73 becomes:

\[ \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R \Phi_R \leq B_i^n \Phi_i^n - \Phi_{i-1}^n B_{i-1}^n + \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_{i-1}^n \Phi_{i-1}^n \tag{5-74} \]

Another condition is also imposed on \(B_R \Phi_R\) by looking at the control volume segment centered at \(i+1\). Using similar reasoning as above and assuming that \(U_{RR} > 0\), the other criterion for \(B_R \Phi_R\) is:

\[ \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_R \Phi_R \leq B_{i+2}^n \Phi_{i+2}^n - \Phi_{i+1}^n B_{i+1}^n + \left[\frac{UB\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]_{RR} \Phi_{i+1}^n \tag{5-75} \]

These criteria would be altered appropriately if the function were monotonically decreasing rather than increasing.

docs.title: Vertical Implicit Transport
docs.text:
Focusing on vertical advective and diffusive transport, constituent transport can be written as:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(BD_z \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z}\right) = RHS \tag{5-76} \]

where \(RHS\) represents horizontal transport and all sources/sinks. Integrating the transport equation vertically and over time gives:

\[ BH\Phi^{n+1} + \theta H \Delta t \delta_z (WB\Phi^{n+1}) - H\Delta t \delta_z \left(BD_z \frac{\partial \Phi^{n+1}}{\partial z}\right) = BH\Phi^* \tag{5-77} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi^*\) = all \(n\)-time level horizontal and explicit vertical transport and sources/sinks
  • θ = time-weighting for vertical advection; 0 for fully explicit, 0.55 for Crank-Nicholson, and 1 for fully implicit

Expanding the differential operators in terms of central differences and collecting terms, the above equation can be recast as:

\[ A_{t_i} \Phi_{i-1}^{n+1} + V_{t_i} \Phi_i^{n+1} + C_{t_i} \Phi_{i+1}^{n+1} = D_{t_i} \tag{5-78} \]

where:

\[ V_{t_i} = 1 + \frac{\Delta t}{BH_{k,i}} \left[ \theta \left( \frac{W_{k,i} B_{b_{k,i}} - W_{k-1,i} B_{b_{k-1,i}}}{2} \right) + \frac{B_{b_{k,i}} D_{z_{k,i}}}{\overline{H}_k} + \frac{B_{b_{k-1}} D_{z_{k-1,i}}}{\overline{H}_{k-1}} \right] \] \[ A_{t_i} = \frac{\Delta t B_{b_{k,i}}}{BH_{k,i}} \left( \theta \frac{W_{k,i}}{2} - \frac{D_{z_{k,i}}}{\overline{H}_k} \right) \] \[ C_{t_i} = -\frac{\Delta t B_{b_{k-1,i}}}{BH_{k,i}} \left( \theta \frac{W_{k-1,i}}{2} + \frac{D_{z_{k-1,i}}}{\overline{H}_{k-1}} \right) \]

The coefficients are computed once, stored in arrays, and used to update each constituent. This is accomplished by loading the explicit part of the solution, \(\Phi^*\), with each successive constituent and inverting the resulting matrix via a Thomas tridiagonal solver.

docs.title: Part 3: Model Input and Output File Descriptions
docs.text: This section of the User Manual describes all model input and output files for CE-QUAL-W2. Each file's format, required variables, and usage context are documented in the chapters that follow.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
1. Introduction: Overview of input and output file categories and command-line working directory specification
  2. Input and Output Files Data Description: Complete descriptions of the control file, all input file formats, and all output file formats
  3. Using Particle Transport: Input file w2_particle.csv and particle transport output files
  4. Using Multiple Processors: Running a cascade of waterbodies simultaneously on separate processor cores using w2_multiple_WB.npt
  5. References: Literature cited in Part 3

docs.title: Introduction to Input/Output Files
docs.text: This part of the CE-QUAL-W2 User Manual describes all model input and output files. Each file's format, required variables, and usage context are documented in the chapters that follow. Input and output files use either fixed-format text or comma-separated value (CSV) text. Output files are typically comma-delimited, with the exception of a few fixed-format output text files.

docs.title: Input Files Overview
docs.text: CE-QUAL-W2 requires several categories of input files to define the model domain, boundary conditions, and simulation options. Figure 1 provides a schematic overview of the input file structure.

docs.title: Required Files
docs.text:
The following files are required for every CE-QUAL-W2 simulation:

  • Main control file: w2_con.npt (fixed-format text) or w2_con.csv (comma-delimited, introduced in Version 4.21)
  • Grid bathymetry file: defines the computational grid geometry
  • Shade file: provides topographic and vegetative shading information

For detailed format specifications, see Input and Output Data Description.

docs.title: Required Boundary Condition Files (Time Series)
docs.text:
• Inflow files: flow, temperature, and constituent concentrations
  • Head boundary files (if applicable): head, temperature, and constituent concentrations
  • Outflow files: flow or hydraulic structure specifications (structure or gate file)
  • Meteorological files: wind speed, wind direction, air temperature, dew point temperature, and cloud cover

Tributary and distributed tributary files can represent either positive (inflow) or negative (outflow) flows.

docs.title: Additional Input Files
docs.text:
Many optional input files activate special routines within CE-QUAL-W2. These include files for:

  • Particle transport (see Using Particle Transport)
  • Total dissolved gas (TDG) and the System TDG (SYSTDG) model
  • Fish habitat
  • Aeration
  • Environmental performance criteria
  • Initial river water level
  • Dynamic zooplankton settling and rising
  • Dynamic algae settling, rising, and toxins
  • Auto-outlet port selection for temperature
  • Sediment diagenesis
  • Dynamic pipe
  • Dynamic gates
  • Dynamic pump
  • Initial conditions (if not uniform)
  • Dynamic light extinction
  • Dynamic structure elevation
  • pH buffering
  • Constriction

Each of these files is described in detail in the chapters that follow.

docs.title: Output Files Overview
docs.text: CE-QUAL-W2 generates many output files during a simulation. The user controls which files are produced and at what frequency they are written. Figure 2 provides a schematic overview of the output file categories.

docs.title: Preprocessor and Model Run Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Preprocessor output: pre.opt, pre.wrn, pre.err
  • Model run output: w2.wrn, w2.err, w2errordump.csv

docs.title: Snapshot Output (Text File)
docs.text: • Snapshot file (SNP): provides a text-based summary of model state at user-specified intervals

docs.title: Binary File for Post-Processing
docs.text: • Visual PLoT (VPL) linkage file: binary file used by w2_post.exe for post-processing model results

docs.title: Time Series, Contour, Profile, and Other Output Files
docs.text:
• Spreadsheet profile (SPR) and longitudinal profile (PRF)
  • Contour output (CPL): Tecplot-compatible contour data
  • Time series output (TSR): time series at specified points or segments
  • Withdrawal output (WDO): time series at withdrawal locations
  • Environmental performance criteria output
  • Initial river water level summary and water level output
  • Dynamic zooplankton and algae settling/rising output
  • Auto-outlet port selection for temperature output
  • Sediment diagenesis output
  • Fish habitat output
  • Flow balance and nutrient mass balance output
  • Kinetic flux output
  • Particle dynamics output
  • W2Anim output

docs.title: Post-Processing with w2_post.exe
docs.text: Post-processing of model output is performed by the user. The program w2_post.exe reads the VPL linkage file and provides tools for visualizing and analyzing model results.

docs.title: Command-Line Working Directory Specification
docs.text:
In the Windows version of CE-QUAL-W2, the user can supply a command-line argument that sets the working directory for both the preprocessor and the model executable. This eliminates the need to copy the executable into every directory that contains input files.

Tip

Use a batch file to run the preprocessor and model sequentially, specifying the working directory as a command-line argument. This allows a single copy of the executables to serve multiple project directories.

In a batch file, execute the following commands:

preW2_v4_64.exe "C:\scott\waterqual\LakeLouise"
W2_v4_64.exe "C:\scott\waterqual\LakeLouise"

The syntax requires the executable name, followed by a space, followed by the working directory path enclosed in double quotes. The executable uses that directory as the working directory for all file operations. The working directory is displayed in the text box of the preprocessor and W2 dialog window during execution.

docs.title: Input and Output Files Data Description
docs.text:
This chapter describes all input and output files used by CE-QUAL-W2 Version 4.5. The model requires a control file and various ancillary input files for bathymetry, meteorology, boundary conditions, and initial conditions. It produces output files for snapshots, time series, profiles, contour plots, kinetic fluxes, mass/flow balances, and diagnostic information.

All input files support two formats unless otherwise noted:

  • Fixed format (space delimited): Fields are F8.0 format (8 characters wide) with right-justified variable names on line 3. The first two lines are comments.
  • Free format (comma delimited): Indicated by a $ character as the first character on line 1. Fields are comma separated with no width restriction. The first three lines are comments/headers.

Free Format Recommendation

The free-format (comma-separated values, CSV) option is recommended for new applications. It removes the 8-character field width restriction and simplifies data preparation using spreadsheet software.

docs.title: Control File
docs.text:
The control file is the primary input file for CE-QUAL-W2. It defines the computational grid, simulation time, boundary conditions, hydraulic and kinetic parameters, constituent controls, and output specifications. Two formats are supported:

  • w2_con.npt: Fixed-format text file with 8-character fields
  • w2_con.csv: Excel/CSV format with the same information organized in worksheet tabs

CSV Control File

When using w2_con.csv, the graph.npt file is not needed because many of its variables are included directly in the CSV control file format.

The control file is organized into a series of "cards," each controlling a specific aspect of the simulation. The following sections describe each card and its parameters.

docs.title: TITLE C
docs.text:
The title card contains up to 11 lines of descriptive text for identifying the simulation. This information is echoed in the snapshot output file and the preprocessor output.

Variable Description TITLE Up to 11 lines of descriptive text (72 characters per line in fixed format)

            Density placed inflow, point sink outflows
            Default hydraulic coefficients
            Default light absorption/extinction coefficients
            Default kinetic coefficients

            Testing sensitivity to wind
            Wind sheltering set to 0.75

docs.title: CST ACTIVE
docs.text:
The [CST ACTIVE] card specifies which constituents are active for each waterbody.

Variable Description Options CAC Constituent active control ON, OFF

The constituents in order are:

  1. TDS (total dissolved solids or salinity)
  2. Residence time (tracer)
